div.head: MY Dram NELLIE,
div.p: MY Dram NELLIE,

It is no longer possible to delay buying a spring hat, for all millinery that has been worn through the winter looks hopelessly shabby in th 3 bright sunshine with which we have lately been favoured. A -very fashionable hat is in deep violet straw, of a nice shade, trimmed with a drapery of forget-me- not blue silk veiled with violet gauze, and a couple of shimmering violet and black quills, while at the back there are a few leaves and a bunch of violets.

fancy straw, - a _ crown of white tulle veiled with black net, embroidered with silver thread, and spangled with sequins. At the side is • cluster of black and white ostrich feathers, held by an oval paste buckle, and under the brim there are several roses of a very becoming shade of pink.
ly _ draped

Prints, flannels, and cambric s are so pretty and inexpensive, and so easily made into unlined shirts and blouses, that every girl should prepare a stock before the actual hot weather commences. For the country or for early morning wear, thin striped flannel, galatea, printed crepon, or drill may be made in blouses of various fashionable styles.

The old favourite, wh/cti is usually termed the "saddle-pattern" blouse is much in vogue. The yoke is lined, and stitched all round, and there is a broad centre-pleat, also lined and stitched down, and fitted with buttonholes. The body portion, cut in three parts, has no lining, and the sleeves, cut in one piece, are unlined. Both collar and cuffs consist of straight bands, as linen ones are generally worn with morning blouses. A very pretty blouse is of white gauze, with a fancy satin stripe in it, and this is mounted on cornflower-blue silk. The vest is of gauged white chiffon, and the revers are of the fancy gauze, edged with tiny ruchings of blue gauze ribbon, which also form a trimming on the sleeves. Every well-dressed woman needs at least one new tailor-made walking costume at the beginning of the season, and now that the fashions change so quickly, many people do not care to pay very high prices for dresses which will be taken imme- diately into wear for all weathers, and which will be put aside after a few months as out of date, when the next new skirt, coat, or sleeve makes its appearance on the horizon of fashion.

A beco iig costume can be made in muslin, lawn, fa...., crepon, or zephyr. With this should be worn a frill of the new open lace, with braid design, and the insertion is of the same type. This makes a dainty gown in cotton crepe, with cream lace, the revers of white silk, and vest of creamy muslin, inserted with lace. The sleeves could be ruffled all up, or inserted with narrow lace, if desired, or a spreading collar could start from beneath revers and fall just over the top of the sleeves.

A new gown is in a tawny coloured joule. The bodice is cut in a square at the neck, showing an unbuttoned vest of sapphire velvet, this again dis- closing a full chemisette of turquoise put de velour. A unique idea la introduced in the cut of the bodice by making the front turn back from left to right, and embroidering the rever thus formed with a fine old cream guipure, used over a facing i of white satin. When the bodice is closed it s secured on the left side by a clasp of bronze, quaintly set with peacock's eyes, and a larger clasp of similar design is also used to secure the Waist- belt of sapphire velvet. A double ruche plaiting of shaded green silks introduces a third colour very prettily at the neck of the vest, and the whole of the bodice and tablier of skirt is braided in a rich design of white silk mixed with threads of gold tinsel. Your loving Jitintia.

div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

The Queen li,oked remarkably well when in town for the purpose of he kilns; the principal Drawing Room of the season. Her Majesty possesses a constitution which seems to defy old age, and lately she has been in better health than for some years past. It was frequently re- marked how well the Queen looked during all the Jubilee festivities nearly a year ago, but by general consent Her Majesty appears younger and stronger than at the time of the Commemoration last June. She is able to undertake long journeys with comparatively little or no fatigue, and fulfil a series of engagements that would try many less advanced in life. Princess Victoria of Wales, though in town with the Princess of Wales and Princess Charles, of Denmark, is still obliged to be most careful not to over exert herself. Her Royal Highness has therefore resigned her place, as her mother's constant companien, to Princess Charles, who, by the way, is apparently enjoying the bcst of health, and her customary high spirits. Princess Victoria will probably proceed to the Continent shortly accompanied by Princess Charles, a change of this des- cription being deemed advisable by her medical atten- dants.

Another Priecess,whose health is causing some anxiety is little Princess Eva of Battenberg. She ia far from strong, and her return via. Calais, from Cimez was de- signed to avoi I the long sea voyage from Cherburg. The little Prince's however will accompany the Queen to Balrooral, and much is hoped frow the spring sojourn on Deeside. _ .

Ia the great palace of Arnsterdare,preparations for the inntallation of Queen Wilhelmina next September are in full swing. The walls of many of the apartments are throughout of Italian marble, and they are new being vigorously scrubbed for the eventful day. Photographs of the young Queen abound in the shop windows,but no palace interiors are procurable, the Kodak is forbidden, and tourists observed to be making notes are severely frowned upon by the palace guard. Queen Wilhelmina has been a monach since her father died, but she can only obtain full responsibility after an installation at the bands of Parliament, a ceremony very similar to that which prevails in Belgium. All the best turned-out Parisians are arranging their hair low in the neck. SOMA of our best known Society women too, have accepted the mode, but the majority will probably cling to their high loops and bows during the present season. Without doubt, it is a great 'deal more comfertable and cleanly to wear our hair high. It keeps tidy much longer, and one's collar, or whatever form of ornamentation we put round our throats, does net become soiled so rapidly. The Princess of Wales and her daughters stili wear their hair in the fashion favoured by them a decade back, but it is a most be- coming one, and, wisely, they refuse to discard it. There are, of course, many eccentricities in hairdress- ing to be seen this season, as indeed there are every year. One girl I espied in a box at the theatre a few evenings back, was the innocent cause of Lonsiderab e amusement. Sn wore a crude red gown, which sloped well off the shoulder., and her hair, parted in the middle was drawn down to form curtainfttes on either side, the remainder being twisted into an untidy looking knet at the back of the head. The girl Zevidently took herself seriously, but the effect was ludicrous. A most fascinating range of muslins. distinguished by an interwoven perpendicular cord, which renders them unusually durable, have made there appearance. There are coral patterns on white and diagonal check*, and well covering spotted patterns of different size, which ' entirely cover the ground work. But the most delightful of all,are the pretty bunches of lilac or rosee, divided by coloured stripe*, like a French wallpaper, and in these and in pretty floral patterns of all sorts, there are the most fascinating varieties. But an item to rernern• , her is—they must be made up over silk. It is a neces• city of our modern times. The turquoise is eni*ying considerable popularity this season, and is far more in demand, among fashionable women, than the ruby. A handsome pendent I was shown at one of our leading jewellers the ether day, the price et which runs in four figures, has a large ere- shaped turquoise in the centre and a border of magnifi- contjeliamonds, but for my own part I must confess that the chill beauty of these pale blue stones a ems always to have something slightly repellent about it. No tur- quoise ornament however magnificent, appeals to mein the same way as the simplest brooch, necklet, or brace- let of diamonds, flashing back a thousand rainbow hues, There are sympathic charms about the deep sea green and the exquisite blue of the sapphire, which of the emerald,you seeit in vain,in the unresponsive porcelainlike surface of even the lovelieet turquoise. Imitation jewels are made in a variety of ways. Us- ually the basis of the paste is an artificially compounded substance called stress, made from litharge, white sand and a small quantity of potash. These ingredients when properly mixed, form the brilliant white Paste from which imitation diamonds are nianufactured. For coloured stones, various additions are made to the white stress. Thus for sapphires oxide of cobalt is added, and for emeralds the oxide of chrome and copper. It may interest many of my readers to know that among the ancient Romans, the men as well as the women wore bracelets, but the latter never wore them till they were betrothed. Bracelets were at first pro- perly military ornaments, or rewards, frequently con- ferred among the ancient by generals and princes, on those who behaved gallantly in fight. They became afterwards arbitrary decorations, assumed at pleasure, and are sometimes said to have been worn for health as well as ornament, and perticularly as amulets to break the force of charms and fascinations. Woolen winter garments should be beaten with a pro- hat of plaited cane, before they are put away. Nothing less will free them from dust, and nothing is so favourable to moths as dust. Beat the garment with the bat, and as the dust rises to the surface, brush it away. If my readers will try this on any coat, however clean it may appear, they will be aetmiched to find how , much dust they will extract or raise. There had been a good many murders, especially of missionaries. That was not an excessive tax, The rebellion arose through the resistance of a chief maned Bey Burral. He intended to despatch a Special Commissioner to inquire into the whole of the cir- cumstances on the spot. After some further debate the motion was, by leave, withdrawn.—The House afterwards went into Committee on the Budget resolutions, and passed the resolution imposing a duty on tea. The motion for the second reading of the Vaccination Bill was,after some debate, Carried by 237 votes to 23. The Select Committee on the Telephorie Service was afterwards appointed. HEIL," proposed an amendment abolishing a poll of the ratepayers as necessary to enable county Councils or corporations of County borough, to promote or oppose legislation.—Afttr some debate Mr. B•LFOUR promised to consider whether some alterrtion in the law could not be made, as he quite saw there was a msteriol difference between a corporetion pro- motleg and a corporation opposing a bill The amendment was withdrawn.—Mr. FLYNN moved that the county boronehs should have the power of dealing with eases where corn nenation for criminal injuries were claimed. div.head: rHE EXAMINER FRIDA Y MAY, 13 1898
div.p: rHE EXAMINER FRIDA Y MAY, 13 1898
" CAPITAL " CHAT.

With the idea, possibly, of increasing the content of the musical public with British instrumentalists, the directorate of the Imperial Institute have in- vited the concert orchestra from La Scala to occupy the bandstand in the gardens for the next three months, The first performance, given on Monday afteruoon,was attended by the Prince and Princess of Wales and the Duchess of York. Heard from the reserved seats in the pavilion,M. Leandro Cam- panari's band of seventy performers, of whom over fifty have been members of the Operatic Orchestra of La Scala,was effective enough for the most part, although to ears accustomed to the best London and provincial orchestras the strings must have sounded decidedly rough. Nor were the brass and reed in- struments by any means up to our own standard. Something, however, must be conceded to a first performance under conditions which were very likely none too comfortable. The bandstand at the Institute is neither in nor out of doors. The Prince of Wales evidently saw the position,and as soon as a ~..onvenient pause occurred he requested the mu- sicians to wear their hats.

There is at present being circulated here an ex- traordinary story regarding an artist whose death was recently reported. A friend of his was dining at a West-end restaurant on eaturday night, and was amazed to find opposite him someone who seemed to him to be the very artist of whose death he had read obituary notices, and with whom he had once spent some time at a watering-place. He mentioned to the supposed artist that his death had been reported, and asked why it had not been contradicted. The reply was simply that it had not seemed worth while. So struck was he with the oddity of the occurrence that he stretched out hie hand, and touched the man to make sure that he was real.

The case of ex-Detective Ostime of the District Railway is certainly one of the most astounding en record. Here was a man in charge of the company's police, passing for a stern and indefatigable enemy of the Railway pickpockets, but all the time en- gaged in leading, abetting, and shielding the very rascals he was employed to catch. According to the evidence of Perry, the pickpocket convict who shared the " swag " with Ostime, there was an arrangement in 'virtue of which he, Perry and his accomplices worked the line underOstime's auspices. They offered Ostime £6 a week for the good will of the business, but the detective elected to go halves in the booty, and out of one month's operations he received as much as £2O. Mr. Detective Ostime might be atilt pursuing the congenial work of the protecting travellers en the underground if he had not been so short-sighted as to peach on his pal who, in his turn, peached on him. It happened in this way. A lady was robbed of her purse in a com- partment containing Ostime, Perry and another confederate. The three were placed together in a room at Victoria. Ostime the virtuous being left in charge by the railway people, who, of course, trus- ted him entirely. But somehow the two men broke away, and Perry was only arrested a few months later. He was identified at the station by his old colleague—who explained to him afterwards in con- fidence that he would not have given him away but for his belief that the police inspector had spotted him. At the trial it was Ostime's evidence that led to Perry's conviction. Then the forebearing Perry told his story to the police, with the results that Ostime has been eanteuced to one year and ten months hard labour at the Old Bailey.

An absurd and extraordinary struggle continues to be waged between Mr. Gibson Bowles and his tormentors on the Ministerial side of the House. The trophy of war is the corner seat immediately behind the Treasury bench. Throughout this Par- liament Mr. Bowles had retained undisturbed pos- session of the place till about a week ago,when Mr. Macdona accidentally played the part of usurper. Since then other members have persistently tried to capture the seat. One of them actually made his way to the House at seven o'clock in the morn- ing for no other purpose than to forestall Mr. Bowles in reserving the coveted place. His discom- fiture on finding tnat that vigilant campaigner had anticipated him may be imagined. The story goes that the member for King's Lynn was in his place On Monday morning before six o'clock.

-- I learn that, consequent on the recent troubles in the Far East, the Government are donsidering the means of accelerating communication with that region, mainly by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Pacific Ocean. The new Transatlantic mail line to be provided by Messrs Petersen and Tate will give a 20-knot weekly service to Canadian ports, but it is felt that a similar service is needed westwards from Vancouver. It is thought that Shanghai should be put within twenty days of Liverpool by a route running all the way through the temperate zone. The route via the Suez Canal and Singapore is terribly hot, and it is much more liable to interruption in case of difficulties with any foreign Power than the route via Canada.

I have heard a shocking story of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel's meeting in Exeter Hall. It is that whilst the solemn theme of the black man was being dwelt upon with earnestness, and, it is to be feared, at some length, the reprehen- sible spectacle was presented of the Archbishop of Canterbury, Bishop Barry, Sir Richard Temple, and Mr. J. G. Talbot all asleep in a row on the plat- form. Whether or not they slept audibly is not stated. Somebody dropped an unbrella in time to save the Bishop of Winchester from becoming a fifth sleeper of Exeter Hall. If only Mr. Kensit could have been lullabied into that goodly company the incident would have been as pathetic as it was unique.

Visitors to the exhibitions now open may differ in opinion as to" the picture of the year.' But the picture of next year is already determined. For Mr. Orchardson, R.A., is to paint, in one group, four generations of the Royal Family—the Queen, the Prince of Wales, the Duke of York, and Prince Edward of York. The whole group has been com- posed and blocked in; and much progress has been made with the figures of the Prince of Wales and the Duke at York. who have already visited Mr. Orchardson's studio and given him sittings. The commission comes to the painter from the Royal Agricultural Society, of which the Prince of Wales is President. This is the first time that an English artist of first rank has had an opportunity to paint a royal group of the kind; and Mr. Orchardson is quite aware that he will have to challenge compari- son with the Stuart family group by Yandyke. The Queen, when it ha 8 been hinted to her to sit to certain eminent English portrait painters, has hitherto replied in effect, " Non Angli, sed Angell"; and Baron von Angeli has in fact been the favored painter. The Prince of Wales has sat, it is true, to both Mr. Watts, EA., and Bastion Lepage. But the Watts portrait of his Royal Highness belongs to quite another stage of his life. The Duke of York and the young Prince sit for the first time to an admitted master. All things, therefore, promise well for a uniquely interesting picture, for which, we may add, the Queen herself has made arrange- ments within the last few days to give personal sittings.

There was an element of delicacy in the National Liberal Clubl inviting the progressive members of the London County Council to meet the leaders of the Liberal party, since the progressives fought their recent battle on non-political lines, and there- fore without the assistance of the Liberal leaders. The meeting,however,which took place on Wednes- day evening was a great success. Sir William liar- court kook care to aveid claiming any share in the glory of the victory, whilst at the same time most heartily congratulating the victors, lie reminded them of the bill setting up one goverment for Lon- don which he introduced as a member of a Liberal Government many years ago, and assured them that in the maintenance of the integrity of the County Council and the unity of the Government of Lon- don they could depend upon the Liberal party. Sir William only spoke "a few words," the programme of the evening being entirely musical, with no place left for speeches. The guests who crowded the club,would not let Sir William go without these " few words," but when a few enthusiasts, still un- satisfied, also called for Mr. Asquith that right hon. gentleman wisely refused to break through the rule which had been made.

THE WHEEL OF FATE.

By MRS. BAGOT HARTB. Author of "Love's Revenge," "Bianca," "Ths Silver Lining," ac., &c. CHAPTER XL. Grace Vane lay sick unto death. The excitement consequent on Musgrove's sudden appearance at the Vicarage had proved her death- blow. Only twelve hours had elapsed since the great shock of his arrival and the harrowing scene which attended his departure; yet the doctor had just stated that nothing cou.'d stay her faii-ebbing strength. Her husband had been telegraphed for, and was now momentarily expected. "Will Dennis come soon?" she murmured in a weak voice.

- " Yes, dear; it cannot be long before he arriTes now," answered Mrs. Hughes soothingly. "I fancy I hear the carriage corning." Mrs. Hughes rose and looked out of the window. "Yes, you are right," said she; "it is coming, and he is in it. But do not allow yourself to become excited. Keep as quiet as you can. I will just go downstairs for a few minutes and send him up to you." "Thank you," was the grateful reply. Grace shut her eyes and strove to keep down her excitement; but it was a difficult matter, so great was her yearning to see her husband. She could distinctly hear whispered communications being carried on in the hali she surmised that the doctor was telling Denr that her moments on earth were numbered. Would he be sorry to hear it? That question instantly arose in her mind. But before it could be answered the door was slowly opened and her husband entered quietly. "Dennis I" she whispered, joy reflected in her face.

"I came as quickly as I could, he answered, leaning down and kissing her. "I am so glad you hare come—in time," she said in a low voice. Then, after a pause added: "I am dying." She uttered these last words with pathetic resignation, though tears glistened in her eyes. _ _

v"I hope not," he said fervently. "It is best that I should die. Lately, I have yearned for death. Mine has been a sad, weary life, through my own weakness. I am glad to die." For a moment neither spoke; then Grace said: "I want to tell you something—before—my strength is all gone." Her lips quivered, but there was no element of fear in her voice. It was as if that courage which had failed her in life was to be hers in death. "I ought to have told you it long ago," she began again. "It was very wrong of me not to do so. I see it all now. Then she 7-topped, to gain strength. Dennis drew his chair nearer and took her hands in his, as if to sustain her courage and strength. She smiled, and her cold hands clasped his with all the power she could summon. Aye, how small was that power now! After a short pause she continued, speaking with laboured earnestness! "The person who forged your name to that cheque was—Richard Musgrove." "Richard Musgrove!" he echoed, with unspeak- able relief. "Yes; and, Dennis "—here her agitation visibly increased—"must I tell you the name of the person who—who tried to cash it—who personated Miss Treherne ? " _ _ .

"lam afraid I ought to know," he answered with a sinking heart. "Promise to forgive her? " "Yes, I promise." The words were whispered. "It was Ethel." "Ethel I But, how did she obtain a duplicate of Miss Treherne's dress ? " "She wore Miss Treherne's dress. Bella White, Richard Musgrove's half-sister, and the Trehernes' lady's-maid, lent it her for the day. We were 80 terribly poor then. Ethel said she must get some money, and after she was married she would pay it back. Norris was coming home from America to marry her. She was afraid he would not do so if he found out we were so very poor. I sold my engagement ring, but that didn't bring enough—" She stopped suddenly, then added, in a hoarse whisper, full of emotion: "It was all my fault— the trouble about the cheque—for if I had not given her the cheque your name would not have been forged, nor would Miss Treherne have been personated." "How did you obtain the cheque ? " he asked. There was no ring of blame in his voice. "I found it in a book you gave me. I ought to have returned it at once. I don't know why I kept it. Father said one day that it might prove useful. I did not know what he meant then. Can you ever forgive me ? " "You are forgiven already—poor Grace!" He leant down and kissed her.

;;;--k-no-,-,--.:11, I ought to tell you that Musgrove did not want to do it. He was bribed to do it—and—and—" Her voice had become almost inaudible. The power of speech was rapidly leaving her. After a short pause she added, whisperingly: "Must Phyllis know when she grows up, Dennis " "I will do my best to keep all knowledge of it from her," he answered in an unsteady voice. "Kiss her for me—and say good-bye—my baby i I She closed her eyes and lay quite still for a few minutes. Then she drew a deep sigh; with that sigh her poor storm-tossed spirit was wafted to its eternal resting-place on high.

div.head: CHAPTER XLI.
div.p: CHAPTER XLI.

Mr. Treherne sat at his desk, calmly sharpening a pencil, with characteristic accuracy of manipula- tion. Dennis Vane stood opposite to him, leaning against the mantelpiece and resting his head on his hand.

"You have my deepest sympathy, 'Vane," the former said feelingly. "Her death must have been a great shock to you, coming so suddenly." "Yes, it was indeed. I had had excellent accounts from my aunt only the day before, saying how well Grace had borne the journey down. Of course, I knew she was in a critical condition of health, but no immediate danger was apprehended. The end was hastened by excitement." There was silence for a few minutes. It was a hard task that lay before Dennis. To reveal the criminal conduct of his wife's relations was no easy matter. He shrank from it with a feeling akin to cowardice. Mr. Treherne noticed that his visitor was unnaturally nervous, and attributed it to his wife's sudden death. • Meanwhile Dennis pulled himself mentally together, and speaking with quiet deliberation said:

"I have called upon you, Mr. Treherne, not only to tell you of my wife's sudden death, but of a communication she made to me just before the end, with reference to the forging of my name to that cheque." In a few well-chosen words Dennis repeated all that his wife had stated on her death-bed. Mr. Treherne listened to the end without uttering a word, then rose and held out his hand to Dennis.
"It has been bravely told," he said "I have always thought well of you, Vane, but never so well as at this moment."

Dennis took his hand gratefully. "I think, in justice to my wife, I ought to add that these secrets weighed so heavily on her mind that they hastened her end," be said, speaking like a man who knows the worst has been faced. "I know she regretted bitterly not having told me them before we married. It was a natural desire to screen her relations which prevented her doing so. But it is a hard matter for me to feel that I have unwittingly caused incalculable pain to friends at whose hands I have received nothing but kind- ness."

"Surely you are not going to assume the quixotic position of self-accuser, Vane I ",said Mr. Treherne in a tone of mild expostulation. "If ever a man tried to do his duty to his neighbour, you have. A man certainly is answerable for his wife's actions, in a measura; but he certainly need not take upon himself the Vogt of conscience-keeper to all her relations. Matrimony is sufficiently handi- capped already ; if you are going to add that of conscience-keeper to the wife's relations to the husband's other duties, I pity the men of the future. Your poor young wife was in a distress- ingly complicated position, and once she had made a false step by marrying you without telling you about that forged cheque, her position became doubly complicated. Poor thing! she has "aid a heavy penalty for withholding that secret. "She has indeed," said Dennis huskily. 'I should like all the facts I have just told you to be laid before Miss Treherne as soon as possible, and I should be pleased to carry out any suggestiona relative to making them public." ,1 "We will r• ,-isult her at once," said Mr. Treherne, ringing the The intervening few minutes were full of oainful

expectation tor Dennis.. tie crew:Lea seeing tne white, careworn face of the girl whose troubles had been caused by the treachery of his wife's relations. As the door opened he glanced anxiously towards her. It was an ideally beautiful face, though robbed of its former vivacity, that NV/1S turned _towards him. With a feeling of relief I,e noticed that the acute sadness which latterly had characterised the expression had already subsided. Mr. Treherne at once repeated to his daughter poor Grace's death-bed confession. This lie did in a manner as little painful to Dennis as possible. When be had finished he said : "Vane suggests OW we shall dictate means by whic.h the. true 'Taal of the case shall be made public. What course do you wish taken, Gwendo- line ? "

She thought for a moment, then answered: "I should not like all that he hai.revealed so bravely and straightforwardly to us, to be laid bare before the whole world and-iliscussed by everyone. lam sure you would not wish it either, father. You, who have always taught me to treat others with generosity, will not deny me the right to live the trial down alone—unaided." Here some of her former animation rose to the surface, and she drew herself up. "I should feel its if I were stooping to an act of meanness by allowing the confession of one who has • gone before ' to be made public, in order to clear my own character from lingering suspicion." "I expected that would be your decision," said Mr. Treherne, with a look of satisfaction, "and you have spoken my thoughts—as. I knew you would." Then, turning to Dennis, he added: "I emphatically agree with what my daughter says. Neither she nor I will avail ourselves of the infor- mation you have generously placed in our hands. There are now three people at large who have put themselves within the power of the law ; but I shall not take upon myself the inglorious work of informing against them. My daughter's character is cleared. Those whose dishonourable conduct has drawn us into the recent vortex of trouble may escape punishment but they will be haunted for ever by fears of their infamy becoming known. I do not envy them in either case. Bella White left our service abruptly yesterday, and there is little doubt that fear of being arrested led her to do so. As for Musgrove, he may be arrested at any moment. Probably the person who personated Gwendoline will never be brought to justice, but in any case I shall not act in a manner that savours of revenge. However, it is quite impossible for ins to express my sense of the high manner in which you, Vane, have acted throughout this trying time. No man could have felt more keenly his own responsibility. For your consideration and great assistance during our recent anxieties you have my most cordial thanks." .

-- "And mine too," added Gwendoline quickly. "You are shewing greater kindness and leniency to me and mine than we deserve," said Dennis in a low, husky voice. Then, as if he dared not face a prolonged ordeal, he added abruptly: "Good-bye, Miss Treherne." "Good-bye." There was a tremulous ring in her voice.
Mr. Treherne grasped his hands warmly. "We must always be friends, Vane," said he.
CHAPTER XLII.

Six years have passed since the incidents recorded in the last chapter, but Mrs. Hughes does not appear five years older as she sits erect, knitting in hand, listening to Miss Mac Alister's troubles and glancing from time to time across the Leas at Folkestone.

"She is so very independent and quick of move- ment, is Phyllis," said the latter, an angular spinster of about forty. "I can't keep her at my side. Yesterday she went off and played on the wet sands with some very worldly-looking children. I motioned continually for her to return, but she only laughed and ran into the sea with her boots and stockings on. I haven't the least authority over her."

"Dear me!" observed Mrs. Hughes in a dis- tressed voice. She had tried hard to bring up Phyllis as a pattern child, and had secured the services of trustworthy Miss Mac Alister to assist. her. Yet here was the old Adam—at least the old Eve—rising to the surface, just as if Phyllis had been godlessly brought up. At this moment the door was suddcnly thrown open, and in walked, or, to speak more correctly, darted, Phyllis. "So, auntie, you have come. I'm so glad!" she cried in a joyous voice. "Where's dad? " she added, glancing round with a look of disappoint- ment.

"He will be here in a few minutes, my dear. He said he preferred walking from the station." "Who would believe, to look at her now, that. her hair was well brushed and neatly tied back just before she went out? " said Miss Mac Alister apologetically, eying Phyllis with marked dis- approbation. "I don't like tidy hair," said Phyllis decisively; and pulling off her hat, she shook her head until her mass of wavy golden hair danced round her like a moving halo. "And oh! auntie, I do want to wear shorter frocks, like other children do. I can't run about and kick in this one."

Mrs. Hughes looked at the anciently-made dress reaching down to the ankles and small tight sleeves with complete satisfaction, then said, almost. severely : "Little girls should not want to kick about." "But I do," answered Phyllis, unabashed. "I've got a picture "—she commenced fumbling in her pocket—" of someone dressed like I want to be." Here she produced a cartoon from Punch of a ballet-dancer in tights and a frill round her waist. " That' s how I should like to be dressed. I could run about easily then." Mrs. Hughes gasped and looked unutterably shocked.
"That style of attire is not decorous for ladies," she said decisively. "Everyone would think I WaS----"

"Oh, auntie," Phyllis interrupted, "I didn't mean that you should dress like that! " Mrs. Hughes dropped her knitting and blushed. :She was speechless with horror at the mere suggestion. "It wouldn't suit you at all," continued the irrepressible Phyllis. "It's me that would look all right in that kind of dress. I'll keep the picture and shew it to dad, and ask him what he thinks." _

"You must do no such thing, Phyllis. Your father would be quite as shocked as I am." "Would he really ? Then I'll tear it up; I shouldn't like to shock dad. Oh! auntie, Tire made some friends—some great friends—on the beach—Eric, Dennis and Conny Hume. Ido love Eric! He and me are going to get married when we've grown up. Oh! here's dad coming. I must go and meet him! " Off she ran, calling out: "Dad, dad, I'm coming ! " as she skimmed across the Leas. He caught her in his arms and kissed her. Then he asked if she had been "a good girl." "No; I never am, Miss Mac Alister says," she replied cheerfully. "But I want you to come a walk with me now at once, dad. I've got a surprise for you—a real, grand surprise. Come along! " She seized his hand with her small strong fingers and began pulling him onward. "We must go to the end of the Leas, then down the cliffs, before we come upon the surprise," said she. •

"I hope it's nothing dangerous—a tiger or lion, for instance ? " replied her father, smiling. "Oh, no!" laughed Phyllis merrily, shaking her golden head. They were soon at the end of the Leas. Then Phyllis pointed down the cliffs to a little ledge, where an artist's umbrella could be seen. "I m an artist," she continued proudly. "The surprise is a big picture I'm painting. The lady under the umbrella is awfully nice. She's lent me paints and brushes—and oh! it's grand fun, dad. I've put a blue sea, and a red sky, and a beautiful yellow sun, and nice bright green fields. You'll like it, dad." There was not a tinge of doubt in her voice.

"I'm sure I shall," he said. "Why do you smile? " she asked, looking straight up into his face. "I was only smiling at the description of your picture. What is the lady's name? "he inquired, in a low voice, for they were now quite near her. "Tree—or something like that." "Not Treherne ? " he asked with sudden interest. "Yes—that's it. And she's been living for a number of years amongst black people. She likes niggers." Then in a louder voice she added: 'l've brought dad to see my picture !" A moment later Dennis Vane and Gwendoline Treherne were shaking hands, for the first time since they had parted the day after poor Grace's death.

"This is an unexpected pleasure! I had not the slightest idea that you were back in England! " said Dennis; and his way of saying it revealed that he was intensely glad to meet her again. "I only arrived in England last week. Constance was ill and wanting change and rest, so I volun- teered to come back earlier than I intended, in order to liberate her from family cares."

"1 Man t trunk you knew each other,- said Phyllis,. eyeing them in a wideawake manner. 'But, dad, you haven't looked at my picture yet," ihe continued in an aggrieved voice, taking hold if his hand. "I put in the fir:iires this afternoc","

"I think I will look at Miss Treherne's first, was the reply. "Oh, don't! It isn't nearly finished yet. There are some parts without any colour on at all, snd mine's covered with paint." "Phyllis is a very energetic artist," said Elwendoline, laughing. "But just look at my men and women! ,eir• they not good, dad? said the small artist referred to, pointing at some elongated one-line figures. "They are rather thin," remarked her father, =fling. "Oh! do Tou think so? I'll make them fatter, !hen. That s easy enough." She spoke with that dauntless courage which belongs to youth. Making them "fatter" provided Phyllis with !,ongenial occupation for a few minutes, during which Dennis said in a low voice to Gwendoline :

"Have you heard the news about Musgrove that is in this evening's papers?" "No." "It appears he was killed in a brawl with some sailors at San Francisco a few weeks ago. He has seen passing under an assumed name." "Why do you look so serious, dad?" asked Phyllis, glancing round. "Don't you like Miss Treherne's picture?" "Yes, I like it immensely," he answered, looking at the dreamy summer scene that Gwendo• line had depicted: "As much as mine ? " queried Phyllis. "Comparisons are odious," he replied. "I don't know what that means. But Ido like my red sky." It was impossible not to laugh at her naive way of admiring her own work. Then cormrsatioa drifted to Gwendoline's travels, and shsogave en amusing account of some of her adventures. "Then you have really had a very pleasant time abroad?" said Dennis by way of conclusion. "Yes; but I have often longed to come home and see everyone." He looked at her for a moment in a sympathetic, understanding manner, then said: "Perhaps we may have the pleasure of meeting on the Leas this evening?" "Yes, I hope so. I generally go out for a stroll in the evening." Then they parted. But it was one of those pleasant partings over which hovers the certainty of meeting again. It was nine o'clock before Gwendoline had kissed her little nephews and niece good-night, and heard them lisp their prayers for "Dada and mudder on de udder shide of the shea." Then she went for her customary stroll on the Leas. Before many minutes passed Dennis joined her.

"I have been waiting for you a long time," he observed in a bond-fide manner. She smiled. It was pleasant to know he was determined to take up his former position of friendliness. At first conversation reverted to Gwendoline's travelling experiences and the people she had met, including some friends of his. "Your fame as a rising barrister has even reached Samoa," she said. "I am glad someone was kind enough to remind you of my existence," lie remarked, laughing. Now that conversation had entered a personal groove the confidential strain of former years asserted itself. "Are you remaining at Folkestone for long?' asked Gwendoline. "I came with the intention of only staying a few days. But now I may remain longer. The matter rests with another to decide." He looked towards Gwendoline as lie said the concluding words, then added: "Would you like me to stay?" "Yes," she answered gently. He took her hands. "Gwendoline," he began in a voice full of emotion, "I have loved you long and dearly—more dearly than I have dared to con- fess to myself durimr your long absence from England. Sometimes f have feared we might never meet again. I will not attempt to describe nil feelings at those times." After a pause he said, in a lower voice: "Have you often thought of me?" 1' There have been few hours when I have not thought of you, Dennis," she answered. "Is my love for you returned? "Yes.' "And have you forgotten the past sufficiently tr be my wife—to bear my name? " He spoke hesitatingly. "Yes. The sadness of the past is all forgotten. There remains to me only the recollection of your goodness and courage." [Tn. Exp.]

div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
THE ALDE MANIC VACANCY.

--- k meeting of the C..‘i cii was held in the Council Chamber at the Toter] 11,11, Warrington, on Tuesday 7ef inc. The Mayor (Alderman Wright) presided, end t.ere were also present :—Alderman Fairclough (deputy ;34a,Yot), Aldermen Sutton, Francemb, Hutchinson, °'tfal Councillors H. Roberts, Shaw Green. Connell. e tailu ropy)°, Smethurst, William Pierpoint, lemeton. eanett, Evans, Ellison, Duncan, Burton, Fornoes, Tinrijoo, Peaeocke, F. R. Roberts, Grace. Woods, Wilkinson, ShOlcock, Monks, Heaton, Loe, John R therm, with Mr. J. Lyn Whittle (town clerk), Mr. SOaeley IV' ilson (deputy town clerk), Mr. Fairhurst (borough traasurer), Kr. Longdin (borough surveyor), Mr. Dees {saeitary engineer;, Mr. C. S. Haddock (gas engineer), and Dr. Gornall (medical officer). The Council met half-an-hour earlier than 116113.1 in order to appoint an alderman to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Alderman Greenall. At the outset the Marna said : The first business for, you to transact is the election of an alderman to fill the vacancy caused by the death of the late Mr. Edward Greenall. I think most of you are well acquainted with the Procedure in such elections, but for the information of thme members who have not previously voted in an Illection of aldermen,! may say that no nomination is hateesary or allowable. Every member who desires to :ate must All up a voting paper, or sign the one already ailed up, and hand the same personally to me. Members Win And on the table a voting paper in which the name Councillcr Henry Roberts has been filled in. It has ,imen done in compliance with the agreement mate en the 9th November last, and signed by every member of the Council either on that date or subsequently. THE STATE OF THE OLD RIVEI BED.-HE&TED DISCUSSIONS.

At a meeting of the Rivers Committee it wee resolved, that Mr. R. T. Fairclou,eh be re-appointed to represent the Corporation on the Upper Mersey Nevigatien elsrn- mission. The Cheshire County Ceuncil having called the attention of the committee to the insenitary condition of the old river bed at Wilderspool, and the Medical Officer of Health having reported that the Corporation had for several months since disconnected all sewers and drains from that portion of the river, it was resolved that the Health Committee be requested to take proceedings to compel the Ship Canal Company to abate the nuisance. Alderman ROBERTS, in proposing the adoption of the minutes, drew attention to two matters of importance. Toe first had reference to the sugeested re-appointment of Mr. R. T. Fairclough as the CounclPa representative on the Mersey Commission, and with regard to it the Council would perhaps remember that he had expressed the opinion that whatever appointments the Corporation had within its power to give should be conferred on members of the Conncil. But there was no rule without an exception, and when it could be shown that the in- terests of the town could be best served by a person who happened not to be a member of tbe Council, then the interests of the town should come first,and that particu- lar private person should be appointed. Mr. Fairclough had so far carried out the duties of representative of the Council on the Mersey Commission in a manner beyond all praise. (Hear, hear). He attenchd every meetiog and afterwards sent them a report of the proceedings,and he (Alderman Roberts) believed Mr. Fairclouah was ever ready to carry out any instructions that the River Corn mittee might consider necessary. (Hear, hear). Mr Faircloulh had undoubtedly special qualifications for the work, and he (Alderman Roberts), had pleasure in supporting his nomination to the position. The other matter had reference to the old river bed, arising out of the memorandum addressed to them from the Cheshire County Council. The Coma. cil would remember that for some considerable time they were unable to do anything in connection with the sanitary condition of the river because the sewage from Stockton Heath was poured into it near Wllderspool brewery, and also because seine of the borough sewage found its way there too. The Paving and Sewerage Committee had relieved the Corporation of all responsi- bility by constructing a drain which took tho sewage entirely away from the district and emptied it at another point of the tidal portion of the river. They were now In a position of being able with clean hands to call tho attention of the Manchester Ship Canal Company to the state of the river bed. There was another phase of the question that affected the Council action. When the Manchester Ship Canal Company applied for power to dose the tidal openings the Corporation arranged with them that certain matters should be conceded. All these matters had been carried out honourably with the ex- ception of one and that related to the construction of a penstock and culvert between the old river bed and the river diversion. The Ship Canal Company was quite prepared to honourably carry out that, but they stated that the operation of the tides upon the river and Ship Canal were now, in censequerme of the closing of the tidal openines, very nearly simultaneous, and rendered the conetrnction a the penstock unnecessary. That was their information up to the present. If it was found to ctiblseel the Corporation wcield only be asking for Company constructing this penstock. The q thrown away if they insisted on the Ship Sbniheuoienps the etCTaa ion of the condition of the old portion of the river had never been lost sight of. It had been before the committee constantly, and he did not think they had done anything to forfeit the confidence of the Council. Alderman Surrom seconded. Councillor BENNETT congratulated Alderman Roberts on his elevation to the bench of Aldermen. He thought Company he should oppose rne Alderman Roberts was entitled to it for his services as chairman of the Rivers Committee. (Hear, hear.) He supported the minutes with certain qualifications. If the e that the be d Canalof thi river Patty were to he bs oeld o onfil meant p atth it to the utmost of his power. He thought the Corpora- tion should ask the Company to deepen the bed, and make it valuable for the purposes of navigation. Alderman BOLTON said as a member of the Rivers ras u tti up Committee he thought the Ship Canal Company should he met in a better spirit. The Company had made an offer to fill no the river bed if the Corporation would pay a sum of ao towards the cost. The TOWN CLERK : No finch offer has been made. Alderman BOLTON Mr. Hunter told me in the course of an interview I had with him that if the enrperation would help them in the expense they would fill it up with pleasure: Continuing Alderman Bolton remarked that the vine up if the river bed weuld be • sourse of expense to Me company. It mew them riving, up a timber pond which was a valuable asset,and It would also necessitate the construction and mainten- ance of a fame, to keep people off the company's land. With regard to the agreement which had been alluded to, he (levied that the town had received any benefit. They had had a laybye constructed which was a laughing stock to the commercial part of Werrineten. In rem, ence to the reduction of duets what had the town got ? They had got • reduction of • Penny a ton to Liverpool, and twopence a ton on slates (Oh ! and laughter). That WM the sum total of what Warrington had received by the agreement. Councillor Nonce said Alderman Belton had foreetten to mention pie iron sling with slates. (Lauehter). Councillor Tinnion strongly supported the resolution, and he hoped the cnnaraittee meant business. The eon- ditien of the old portion of the river was a disgrace not only ti the town but alio to the Connell. It wag unrea- sonable to expect that anyone could live in eood health with such a nuisance in the neighbeurhorni. He strongly urged that something should be done to discontinue the nuisance. Alderman Stereos did not see how the Health Com- mittee could move straight away in the chatter, as the Corporation had heed te some extent reop•nsi tee up to within • recent period. There seemed io be a dimposie tiara on the part of the Ship Canal Company to make move in the matter, and to do whatever was reasonable. As long an there was this diepesition on their met to abate the nuisance he did not think they ought to talk about taking proceedinee against the Manchester Ship Canal Crimean,. flaomuld be in favour as Chairman of the liaalth Cqrsnlieree to do all he possibly could to bring about the desired result without proceeding to ex- trernitisse.

Alderman Bourns said the extraordinary pe rferm- soca of Alderman Bolton was really beyond hie compre- hension. Be would like to *new what the Chairmen of the various Committees would think. if when they had a serious natter under consideration' in reyard to which the interests of Warrington were of paramount import- ance and where a serinus principle wag involved, a member of their own Committee went behind the backs of the chairman and vice-chairman and consulted directly with the paetios who were °noosing them. That was the charge he had to make against Alderman Rotten. Alderman Bormox rose to • point of order,and dents I e that he had gone behind the backs of the committee. He did not go al presentativ of the Corporation.but as ono intsrsstsd outside the Borough. Alderman ROURTS (continuing), said that the action of Alderman Bolt,on had put him in a very awkward position, and be shonid decline to take the responsibility of chairman of the committee. if any member went be- hind his back to negotiate with an authority when nego- tiations were already in progress between the officers of the Corporation. They had sow ceased to be contribu- tors to the nuissncs in question, and it was • monstrous key other authority from Its legal responsibility thing to ask the Corporation to sp Ind a shilling in re- lieving in connection with its liabilities. He objected to be a Dirty to take upon his shoulders. CC a member of the Corporation the responsibilities of any othsr body what- ever. They had quite enough to do to manage their own affairs. The Manchester Ship Canal Company had never made the offer alluded to by Alderman Bolton. Re hoped the Council would stand by the Rivera Coin- wide& Alderman BOLTON rose to make an Application. Ho replied that he had not gone behind the committee's back to interfere with negotiations. Ho had interviewed the company when a private resident of Stockton Heath for the purpose of getting some information relating to thsir action in reference to the nuisance from which he was then a sufferer. Alderman ROBIItTe said the interview which Alder. man Bolton referred to in regard to Stockton Heath was one thing ; the interview he (Alderman Roberts) referred to wax another thing and a more recent one. The minutes were then confirmed. INADEQUATE WATRR MAINS—IMPROVEMENTS -------

be a greater no,sibility of their rrquirements beiru: attended to. They had on many occast sws'ed such things VI the alteratiuo of hydrants and m hut their stigvstion: had been treated will very "co it courtesy. The MLYOR : I see no objection to the mn.,u'e :v, it stands. There is no offmce intmde4. Councilor J. SHAW GREEN said there wi.s no reasou given for putting it on the minutes. Councillor PLunrrote said he was surprised C:uncillor Shaw Green should say that. If he looked higher up the page he would find that there had been a fire at Mr. Bennetts' Clap-gate Farm,Lovely-lane. The fire engine went there and on arrival found there was no water. There was only a 3-inch main in Lovely-lane. If the Water Committee would not find the Fire Engine Com- mittee water,how could the Fire Engine Committee be responsible for not putting out any fires that occurred. The people in Lovely-lane should be protected as well as those in any other part of the town, and if there was only a 3-in main the Water Cotnmittee was not doing Its duty by allowing it. Councillor LONOTON thought the Council should not waste time. This was only a request between one corn- mittee and another.
Councillor LE thought that Alderman Hutchinson had been placed on the Water Committee for the exact purpose of dealing with matters such as this.

Councillor SMETHURST spoke in similar terms to Coun- cillor Plumpton. He added that if the wind had been blowing the other way on the occasion of the fire in Lovely-lane the whole of the farm stock and buildings would have been burnt to the ground. Councillor PIERTOINT said he thought it was right that the Water Committee should pay special attention to the mains, and he did not think the Fire Engine Committee should be taken to account for doing what was to the good of the town's inhabitants. He would like to point ' out something with reference to Thel wall-lane. (Oh ! and laughter.) There was a 3 inch main there with not a single fire hydrant in it. He did not say there was very much property, but there was some of his, insured for a considerable sum—say for £40,000. (Laughter.) They might laugh but he assured them it was the truth. In the whole length of Thel wall-lane there was not a single hydrant. In the event of any fire taking place at his works—he had had two, hut none lately—there would be no supply of water from the lane. He had had two hydrants placed on his premises by the Water Commit- tee, but he was rather afraid they were going to make an annual charge for the use of them. (Laughter.) He wou:d rather they had been placed in the lane. He thought it was only littinz and proper that the Fire Engine Committee should be commended for their atten- tion to the means of putting out fires within the borough.

Alderman HUTCHINSON said he believed the minute had been placed on the agenda simply as a recommendation to the Committee. If they found it was not necessary to bring before the Council what they required they would ask the Water Committee to do what they were now submitting to the Council. The minutes of the Committee were then approved. Alderman FRANCOIIII proposed the passing of the minutes ot the Water Committee. In doing so he must say that he did not feel any insult on the part of the Fire Engine Committee for placing this recommendation on the agenda. It cer- tainly would be more complimentary to the Water Committee if they ha I sent the request directly to them and their engineer ought to know a little bit more than the Fire Engine Committee as to what size of pipes were required. In the future they would be pleased to give the Fire Engine Committee's recommendations every consideration. It had been mentioned by his deputy that Alderman Hutchinson had been placed specially on the Water Committee to go from one to the other and enable the two committees to work amicably together. He could assure Councillor Tinnier' that the Water Committee were anxious to do the best they could for the Council and the town generally, and he thought no- body could accuse them of being too proud to listen to complaints front anyone. Alluding to what had been said with regard to Lovely-lane, Alderman Francomb re- minded the Council that they received from the Water Works Company a terrible legacy. They were not com- pelled to find water to put out fires or for manufacturing purposes. Our forefathers were wise enough to get a stipulation put in the Act that they could put hydrants on any of the Water Company's pipes but forgot the size of the pipes, consequently hydrants might be placed all over the town but they would be of no use. If the Council was prepared to give the Water Committee suffi- cient money during the next six or twelve months to put 6 inch or $ inch pipe. down—which were absolutely re- qoired for proper accommodation—they were quite pre- pared to go forward and take the responsibility of doing it. They had to consider the rates. The Water Com- mittee had spent many thousands of pounds during the last 7 years In putting II inch pipes where there was never anything bigger than three-inch. The com- mittee did not wish to make matters too hard upon the ratepayers but they would promise that they would add to the size of the pipes, both in rhelwall-lane and Lovely- lane, and make them sufficient to put ont any fire. Although it had been mentioned that I inch piping was required for Lovely-lane, he might say that they were seriously thinking of putting down an I inch pipe and had given instructions to the Water Etgineer to esti- mate the cost of connecting Lovely-lane. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Francomb concluded by stating that the com- mittee had considered several schemes for the construc- tion of a reservoir for water at Appleton, and had ordered infermation to Ise got with respect to the scheme "A." Thor had not, as stated on the minutes, deckled to proceed with the scheme "A." Councillor LRX seconded the passing of the minutes, which was agreed to.

THE GYMNASIUM. Councillor TINNION proppsed the adoption of the nslnutes of the Gymnasium Committee, and reported that the instructor, Mr. Kinsley, was now almost corn- pletely recovered from his illness. He was pleased to mention that they had now received some 400 or 500 scholars from the People's College, and he hoped that at the end of the month the attendance would be larger and more satisfactory to the Committee.—Counclller Smethurst seconded and the minutes were adopted. Oa the proposition cf the Mayor, seconded by Alder- man Sutton, the rgieutes if the Gen.ral Purp3ses Com- :salmon were passed. VICTORIA PARK—COUNCILLOR ELLISON'S MOTION POSTPONED.

Councillor SELW Gains said that before calling upon Councillor Ellison to move "That the Open Spaces Cot. naittee be requested to make arrangement* fee opening the whole of the front portion of Victoria Park for public recreation purpoaes on and after May 30th, 1898," be would like to say a word or two. Be thought it would be unwise to bring the motion forward because. on the leth meat, a Local Government Board Inspector would be In Warrington hearing their application to borrow£3o,ooo part et which was for widening the road opposite Mis estate. If the motion was postponed it would be a good thing. The MAYOR : I should be glad if Councillor Ellison Could see his way to withdraw the matter for a month. . _ ..
Councillor ELLISON *Fronted the explanation, snd said he had great plessureon the interests of the Council, in withdrawing the motion for the present. The Council then rose.

Dr. Tizauts' Vi-Coco• (1898), LIMITSD.—The Statu- tory Meeting of the Shareholders of the above Company has bees held this week at the Registered Office, 60, 61, and 62, Bunhillitw, 8.C., Mr. Alderman Treloar pre- siding. The Chairman said that the Company acquired the benefit of the trading from the let March last, BO that at the end of April they had just two months trad- ing to review, and he should like to call attention to that brief period. Be had pone over the figures, and he found that, as compared with the corresponding couple of months of last year the sales showed • very large ' increase. The certified net profits of last year were E 72,000, or at the rate of £6,020 per month. The amount required for the preference dividend was £12,000, the profit upen two months' trading. They had already earned more than sufficient profit to pay the whole year's preference dividend. Be was cmfident they would agree with him that they had every reason to be gratified that they were interested in such a suc- cessful tuidertaking as Dr. Tibbles' Vi-Cocoa (1898) Ltd. was likely to become.

TETE GRAMMAR SCHOOL. APPOINTMENT OF A REPRESENTATIVE GOVERNOR.

Alderman FHA/WOMB proposed that the Mayor be elected a representative governor of the Warrington Grammar School. His Worship had been a long time connected with the school.his eons having been educated In it,and took a deep interest in the institution. He be- lieved there was a very close alliance between the Gram- mar School and the Parish Church. and he should be pleased if the Council would elect the Mayor as a governor of the school. The DertrerMaroe seconded the motion ; and re- marked that it had been a custom whenever a vacancy occurred to appoint the Mayor for the time beingit was done in the case of Alderman Greenall, and in his (AldermaniFaircloueh's) ewn case. Councillor PISRPOIHT : Whilst I feel that the Mayor would make a most fitting representative, I should Me to ask whether the rule of seniority applies only to the election of aldermen ? The Marna : I would rather not have anything to say about the matter, but before I allowed my name to be brought forward as governor I pointed out to Alder- man lirancomb and to Alderman Sutton that they were my seniors,and told them that! was willing to give way in their favour. Both of them most graciously said they preferred me to have the office. Councillor POIRPOINT : lain quite satisfied with the explanation. Councillor SMETHURST also supported the motion, and said he was pleased to hear the remarks which had been tintmadeettwe itthhouregshpteetthta h et the previous Mayors. At the same when a vacancy occurred the ap- pointment should be left entirely in the h cede Of the Council. He was pleased to hear that both Alderman ' Sutton and Alderman Francomb were consulted in this noo sastneatenucesteli a.nw odiottuhhnatehti b aelltrseuwatyalluded for the Mayor. In to the Mayor's Church as one reason why he i ooprtahsr Inge cie 00, nn should be appointed a Governor. Alderman Holman said he supported the nomination hut on entirely different grounds from those which had been advanced by some speakers. He quite epprecived the fact that the Mayor's predecessors were eleited governors of the school as representing the Corporation, and the principle was a sound one, as far as the Chief Magistrate was concerned. He did not see why, if the Mayor desired it. he should not be aepointed to such a position but ho dissented entirely—he was a Dislenter—to the aseociation of the Grammar School end the Parish Churchor any other church. The Grammar School woe a public school, it was not a Church of Elgland School, and although certain matters connected with ita curri- culum were associated with the Church of 'Entiand he claimed that it was a public school in the broadest sense of the term. And the present headmaster would be the first to disclaim any primary association with any ecclesiastical organization whatever. houoht that if netting opportunity arose it woweld not be to the dis- advent:me of the institution or to the Council if they were to introduce a little leaven in the shape of one Dissenter. (" No, no.") His friend CounCillor 'Les said "No, no." He should say" Why not r The MAYOR: Don't let us make this a religious ques- tion. If I represent the Council I shall aho represent the whole borough. Councillor ROBIRTS said no one had more confidence in the Mayor's fairness and justice than he had. He I should, however, like to add that one of the first elected governors to represent the Council was Mr.'E 'ward Milner, ano he could not be considered a 'Churchman. There was no disqualification of any bind whatever to any DiSSenter or even a man who did not profess any religious faith whatever, from being a 'representative governor of the Corporation on the Grammar -School management. (Hear. bear.) He did net want it to be understood by the Council that the appointment of three governors bad any connection with the Parish Church.lt was nothing of the kind and was never intended to be so. (Hear, hear). The motion was put by Alderman Francon:lb and unanimously passed. The bravos, in reply, said he should endeavour to represent not only the Connell, hut the whole of the 1 town. He had always taken a deep interest in the in- I stitution, and his two sons had been educated in it. He felt that he owed a debt of gratitude to the head-master for the kind interest he had shown in the education of his sons—especially his eldest son, who now held a good position as mathematical tutor, If the Council would I give him their confidence they would have no cause to I regret it. (Hear, hear.) Alderman fittrrotr, who entered the room while the Mayor was 'peaking, said he supported the motion. He was under the impression that the Council had been summoned for six o'clock, and not for half-past five. That was the reason he was late in coining tcrthe meet- ing. THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.-SATISFACTORY REPORT.

Alderman &Mon moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Health Committee. In doing so he said with the permission of the Council he would like to give the Council a little information supplied by the Medical Officer of Health with respect to the health of the town. The information stated that the general health of the town was good. There was nearly a complete absence ef notifiable zymotic diseases. For the 17 weeks eon- prising the first four months of this year the death rate was 175 per thousand of a population of 62.770—a de- cidedly low rate for the time of the year. The highest death rate in a single week was recorded for the 9tlo week of the year when it was 266, and the lowest was 10'7 in the 6th week. The zymotic death rata for the four months in question was 17, which was also a re- markably low ens. Measles which were frequent during the first three months of the year had nearly dim- appeared. There was no scarlet fever and consequently the staff at the hospital bad had a well-earned rest, and to-day as far as the Borough of Warrington was con- ' cerned the hospital was empty. (ffear.hear.a Alderman ROBERTS seconded the adoption of the minutes. He thought the Medical Officer, and the staff they had at the hospital were to be heartily congratu- lated upon the happy condition of things generally in the town. He wished they could do sornethieg to pre- vent the constant recurrence of measles wltich did 81 much harm, end wale so largely the canes of death amongst young children. Until it became a notifiable disease with the others he was afraid they could not reach it in any satisfactory manner. The minutes were approved of. The Queen has presented a one hundred guinea cup to St. George's Yacht Club, to bp sailed for at Kingstown Regatta, held on July 20 and 21. An anonymcus donor of £l.OOO has endowed a bed in perpetuity at St. Thomas's Hospital, London, in menory of Charles Kingsley. The Rev. Dr. Guinness Rogers entered on the thirty. fourth year of his pastorate at the Congregational Church. Clapham, on Sunday.

The tallest monument composed of a single stone lir at Marbak,in Egypt. It is 108 feet 10 inches high. The Duke of St. Albans died on Tuesday forenoon at Brooke House, Isle of Wight,tbe residence ef Sir Charles Seely.

Fitzsimmons has aecepted Kid ld'Coy's offer to pay him 10,000 dol.. for a Aght at middle-weight, and Corbett's offer of 25,000 dole, for an ..pportututy to re gain the beavy-weight championship. On Saturday serious rioting took' place in Milan, where barricades werA erected across the streets. • state of siege was proclaimed in the city. It is stated that 300 rioters were tilled and 1.000 wounded in con- flicts with the soldiers.
The two men Karditza and Giorgi', who en February le last fired at the King et Greeee on the road between Plialerum and Athens, wen" executed early on Monday morning at the Palamidis Fort.

As the Queen's of the Belgians went driving in the Royal Park of Laeken on Saturday, the carriage was overturned into a lake at a sharp turning. Help waa at once forthcoming and Her Majesty was extricated from her critical position. No serious consequences are appre- hended.

A Brussels Correspondent states that a revolting crime woo committed last week on the highway in the neigh- bourhood of Verviers. A journeyman carpenter shot a young girl aged fourteen, whom he met casually, and after inflicting mortal wounds dragged the body into a neighbouring thicket. The *swain, who appears to be a homicidal maniac. was *treated en Saturday after fur- ther murderous attempts en several other persons.

Sixty members of a lied known by the name of Advendiste assembled on the sands, where an open- -1 air service wan held, followed by a public haptiam (by immersion) in the waters of the German Ocean. Reuter's Agency is informed that in exercise of the right reserved to the Chinese Government by the Treaty of Shimonoseki of paying the outstanding portion of the p war indemnity by a mini,ayment at the end of the third year from May 5, MB, instead of by means of equal annual instalments extending until the seventh , year, the balance of the indemnity and one year's occu- pation expenses of Wei-hai-Wei were paid to the Japan- ese Government at the Bank of England at a little be- fore noon on Saturday. Sir Halliday Macartney and Mr. Lo represented the Chinese Minister, and Mr.Koike Ithe Japanese Minister, in making the payment, which, lin view- of the largeneass or the amount, £11,001,857 les. 9d., wes made in the presence of the Governor, the Deputy Governor, and the chief cashier oi the Bank. Tea transaction really involved a sum of nearly thirteen million sterling, the difference being settled in *moot. The payment Vgl.l made by a single cheque, prebahly the largest that was ever drawn on , the Bank of England. The above-mentioned payment haapvainnit o been China under transacted. all pecuniary claims of J under the Treaty of Shimonoseki have now been settled, and China is entitled to demand the withdrawal of the Japanese forces from Vrei-hai-Wei.

There is however, no definite declaration that the obnoxious hut-tax 'shall be abolished, and in dealing with ignorant natives of; certain countries there is always it, aunpicion of pedantry attached to the official fondness for re-- asserting authority beforedisposing of a grievance This a time-honoured, formula, and it has Lean. responsible for many wars: Rimier() the grievance and there will Often be no furthEir,!'difficulty in re- asserting authority. That the nations of Sierra Leone should develoPsOinticli intensity of revolt.',' has come upon this country as a surprise.- Bu 3 there are few colonies in which the native races , preponderate ht are not it one .time or another exposed to the machinations of malcontentsi.who may , have persOnal ends in view. It .is one of the dangers which- the British ad- ministration has to Carefully guard against;' for experience with native races has repeatedly im- ,prosE„ed upen European authorities the truth that to give way to the forces .of disorder, even ,on a 'comparatively small :point; is to prepare the' way for More serious trouble. Yet, sup Posin- the hut- tax tn be at the root of the evil it is not unreason- able to sudst that the readiest way of quieting. the peoplawould be to, abate _the. .Objectionable impost. This s an idealrwhich does not find easy admission to the .official , Mind. The difficulty' really lies in the occasional: inability to criminte between the original causes of the upheaval and those introduced. at. it later st 43, of _development. The disturbances in Sierra Leone ePeedllY became complii:iated, and it was evidently no part: ofrithe resistance to the hut-tax to murder missionaries and destroy mission staticns: Yet this is what hap- pened, and. it is worthy of note in this connection ' that some of the ,missionarien: .murdered were Americana. Sierra' Leone 'is England's eldest -African colony, being 'Peopled by blacks, rescued from slavery and seribto the country from r many- parts of the world,to:iiihabi,t put-plaCe now known :as Freetown. Large lumbers of these blacks .are ; .in tlq) eertice of the English Government,. and . . , many ef them .display . considerable nite,lligence. British ciffiser has .7been despatched to Freetown, while according to the latest intelligence,lmperial white troops are being sent out, and two companies of the West' Indian 'troops embarked at Lagoa this. week. All the Europeans in the .celpny are under arms,' the 'Kinglets who had previously-fought on the side of the authorities against the rapacity of certairr ; Marauders from the interior havingnumed a hos- tile attitude,' arid it it affirmed' that one chieftain 'alone has meowed to raise'n'force of between five ,and six thousand -men; *". of the kind, but the plan officially suggested was characterised by the employers as one-sided. hen, it is a peculiarity of the South Wales coal eld that it coes not yield sufficiently accurate data for the striking of averages in connection With other coal-,fields. The south Wales miner does not work so much as he might; and having regard to the nature of his 'task he is, perhaps, not to be much blamed. But it is a fact that many coal-getters often labour only three or four fir five days a week, and keep holiday on the other (laYs. This effects the output, and renders Practically abortive any attempt to compare the earnings in the South Wales .fields with the earn- ings of colliers in other districts. In ' effect it requires more men in South Wales to raise a Riven quantity of coal within the same period than it does elsewhere. In the cases of the Board of Trade returns for a recent period it was shown that within a given time 47,685 under- qround workers in Durham raised 21,933,211 tons Of ; and in the !LIMO period it took 54,560 Persons in South Wales to raise 20,458,398 tons. This shows that though the South Wales miners may think themselves badly off as compared with the workers in other fields, it may not be so. That the question is complicated willbe admitted, and the complication ii added to by the intervention Of a monthly holiday. After " Mabon's Day" several other days usually elapse before the whole force of men have taken up the routine of their labour,and this occurs twelve times a year, thus aPpreciably increasing the cost of production as Well as materially reducing the output. The in- atitution is local, and it would be better for the Miners themselves if it were relegated to the [hobo of other obsolete observances. There were ettrernely ominous signs at the outset, and both swners and workers would have done well to have taken them more seriously into consideration be- fore adopting the miserable policy of war. Some Of the miners' best friends advised them to accept Provisional terms, with the view to keeping the collieries open, and to utilise the interval in per- fecting their organization and filling their war- chest. If this modus-operandi had been proposed it was believed that the ,pviiers would have agreed to it. Something is usually gained by delay when questions at issue more towards an acute stage, Ind the hitterneS3 of actual confiet is avoided. As it is, however, the nitterneqs, has been experienced and despitis'. the fact that liberal contributions have bsen made to the strike fund, the absence of the well-fiffed archest has been felt. - Privation indeed been working havoc in the South Wales coal field,and whatever may be the measure sl* sYrnpathy with the dissentient colliers, it is clear that thefinancial reserve at their disposal has al- ready dwindled dovril. to a dangerously low point, mad the result is that not only miners but inde- Pendent industries, and traders as a rule,are suffer- ing considerable smlaarrossment.

A TRAMP AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday Morning, Edward Bradley, a tramp,was brought, up before Mr. Ockleston, J.P., chargisd with begging at Runcorn, and was sentenced to 14 days' im- prisonment.—lnspector Hicks proved the case. EFFIICT or THE GALE AT WIDNES. , On Wednesday, a portion of a large marquee, which had been erected near the Parochial Schools, Widnes, for the purpose of holding a three days' bazaar in connec- tion with the St. Paul's Church, was blown down. The damage done was not, however very great, and it is reported there were not many damagable articles under the portion that collapsed. teo far as can be ascertained no damage to pr )perty or life has occurred in Runcorn and district truce the effect of the great wind of Wed- nesday. AN ALPEAL IN A WORTHY CAUSE. .

On Sunday, May 15th, two sermons will be preached in fialton-road Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn by the Rev. Edwin Owen, in aid of a scheme for the extension of the Old Mill Brow Wesleyan Sunday School. The services will be held in the morning at 10.30, and in the evening at 6 o'clock. The scholars and choir have been rehear- sing special inimical compositions by Frost and Judajor the occasion, which promises to be a most interesting gathering, and will at the same time be the celebration of the anniversary of the Sunday schools,but the feature lof the musical portion of the services will undoubtedly be the solos of Miss Clara Taylor. The friends of the cause make this especial appeal, and an opportunity of siding the work is given, with a gentle hint not to for- get the silver collection. For details see advertising columns.

DEATH Or A PROMINENT CHURCHMAN. At the Parish Church, Runcorn, on Sunday last, the Rev. W. Scholes, alluded in the course of his sermon. to the loss the church had sustained in the demise of Mr. Thomas Nicholls. The Rev, gentleman said so staunch and sincere a Christian ; so loyal and upright a man, was he, that those who knew more of his inner life might well say of him, Llfe's race well run. Life's work well done. Life's crown well won; Now comes rest." God grant that it was so; perfect rest and happiness in the nearer presence of God, a taste of that calm, beanty and happiness, that belonged to the &lurch triumphant in the paradise of God. - ' 0.1 CRUEL NEOIXCT Cirrinacri. SOCIETY. At Sunday's meeting of this Society, there was a good attendance, when the Rev. Joseph Osborne, 8.A., (presi- dent) occupied the chair. The speaker the Rev. C. Christien, of St. Paul's Wesleyan Church, R in- corn, ana in his eloquent address bC referred to the ad- vantage which was to be gained by setting before them- selves a high ideal of Christine life. This not only resulted in happiness to themselves, but also secured to them the respect and confidence of their fellowmen, and contrlbated to the well-being of all. Amongst the musical portion of the meeting the solos " Cathedral Voices" by Mr. T.Worthington,and "Charity" by Miss Jennie Rogers were well received ; whilst Miss Agnes White's recstation of Clifford Barrison's well-known poem tt Faithful unto death " was received with warm ecomiums by the highly. appreciative audience.
