ROEDER"! FROIL A WIDNES FLAT. At Widnes PAic Court on Tuesday, before Alderman W. W. Gossage and Major Lewis, two young men named John M'Keever, Pitt-street, and Theophilus Whitaker, John-street, were chaeg,ed with stealing a pair of sea boots and two flannetlhirts, vallui 30s, the property of John Full, mate of the fiat Rosette. Prosecutor met , both prisoners at the Round Heise beerhouse, Widnes, lon Friday last. He left them and went on board the Hit, leaving his bag containing the articles in the galley. Full then went back to the Round House, and on return- ing to the flat soon afterwanis he found both prisoners in the galley. After they had left he made an examina- tion of his bag, and found that the boots and shirts were missing. Police-constable Thornton apprehended the prisoners on Monday afternoon. They admitted taking the boots, but not the shirts.—Both men having good characters, the magistrates at first sentenced them each to fourteen days' imprisonment, but, some friends of the accused having asked for the infliction of a flee, they were ordered to pay a guinea or fourteen days. WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL. •

The monthly meeting of the above council was held on Tuesday, the Mayor (Alderman Wareing) presiding. On the health committee's minutes coming up for con- firmation, the following resolution with regard to the proposed infectious diseases hospital was passed : " That the plans and estimate' amounting to £7541 be apnroved and adopted, and that application be made to • the Lecal Government Board for sanction tai the borrow- ing of the amount required to carry out the works as stated."—lt was agreed to levy a general district rate lof 23. 21. in the pound.—Councillor Shores moved the following resolution :—" That the parliamentary and general purposes committee be instructed to make in- lqeiries as to the relative cost of policing the borough— (l) by the present arrangement with the county and (2) ,as a separate police force for the borough ; and to report to the town council as to whether any, and if any what action should;be taken in the matter." He said the question was raised because the general purposes committee had noticed an increase in the charge for policing the borough. The charge had increased from £1575 in 1892 te £2248 in 1897. He produced figures showing that it would possibly, redness the, rate for the police 14. its the pound. The reifolution was carried. ' SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY OF THE PRIMITIVE METHODISTS. • In connection with the Primitive Monodist cause.of this town, there is a most. successful Sunday school; which has exerted a great influenee for good within tha district. That the cause is a prosperous one will be seen from the fact that there are over 243 scholars Upon the school register, with an average attendancesfor the year of 178 The anniversary of the school was fittingly cele- brated on Sunday and Monday last, when special ser- vices were hell. Commeecing on Sunday morning with service in the large and capacious chapel in Greenway Road, the proceedings exthuled throughout the day and concluded on Monday evening. Eleqeent and stirring sermons were preached to large' congregations by the Rev. J. Travis, of Oldham, an ex-president of the con- ference and the Rev. S. Wright, ese-oresident of the United Methodist Free Church Conference. Special hymns were sung appropriate to the encl. sion, and tor the efficient training of the children in their musical portion of the service great praise is due to Mr. Gittinge, who also presided at the organ, a duty discharged with his usual ability. Anthems were rendered by the choir, the principal solo- ists being the Misses Hillidge,and Mr. Ambrose Shingler. —On Monday evening a service of song entitled " Tim's S3crifice " was rendered by the scholars assisted by the members of the choir, Mr. A. R. Norman, J.P., acting as reader of the conneotive parts. The piece was most enjoyahle throughout and reflects great credit upon the promoters It passed off without the slightest bitch end so far nothing hut what is complimentary has been said about the concert. The whole of the meetings proved most successful and the collections, which will hr, dps voted to the Sunday School fund, amounted to about £34 showing, if anything, an advance on the amounts for previous yeare. BRICE!. AYERS AND THEIR WAGES. The master bricklayers in ansteer to the request of the workmen at Runcorn, for an advance of i. an hour in wages.and time and a half whilst working overtime,have declined to concede the increase,but decline to grant the concession with regard to overtime. The workmen, however, have accepted the terms,and the notice which they gave to the masters will not be colored. Sr. JOHN' TEMPERANCE A EISeCIATION. On Tuesday evening an interesting essay was delivered by Mr. Henry Acicerley on The words and works of Christ bearing witness of Him," The essayist observed that even the words and works performed and uttered by Christ proved Him to be a true messenger sent from God, and that through Him theta might have eternal lire. The works of Christ were works of wonder, works of sympathy, tent-ling to the benstit of nsankind. A short discuseion followed, anti a few remarks by Messrs. J. Richardson, T. Leach, and F. Littler brought an enloyable evening to a close. ear

RUNCORN BOARD OF OUARDIANS.

--- The fortnightly meeting of the above Board was held on fuesday afternoon at Dutton Workhouse, Mr. J. Mosely Williams presiding. There were also present Messrs. S. Taylor J.P.. A. R. Norman, J.P., S Yarwood, and J. Meadewcroft, with the members of the Rural District Council, ani Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), Mr. G. F. Ashton (deputy clerk), and Mr. J. Cunnah (workhouse master).

div.head: LADIES VISITING COMMITTEE.
div.p: LADIES VISITING COMMITTEE.

Miss Mallinson of South Bank, Frodsham, wrote de- clining to serve on the Ladies Visiting Committee, on account of tailing health.—lt was decided to write to Miss Mallinson thanking her for her past sorvicei. and regretting that she could not see her way to allow her- self again to be elected.—Mr. Woodward moved that he would name a lady at the next meeting. DR BOWER'S DErETY. Dr. H. E. Bower, of Stretton, wrot3 stating that he had appointed Dr. S. .1. Parker, of Stockton Heath, in the place of the late Dr. Starkey Smith of Warrington,to act as his deputy. He hoped this would be ratified by the Board.—The appointment was confirmed.

div.head: WORKHOUSE CHILDREN AND DUTTON BOARD SCHOOL_
div.p: THE WORKHOUSE CHILDREN AND DUTTON BOARD SCHOOL_

Mr. Charles E. Linaker, clerk to the Dutton School Board, wrote stating that he had pleasure to state that bis Board had decided to fix Monday next, the 18th inst as the date when the children from the Union might be received The Board had sufficient room for the whole of the children. It was understood that all the children including the infants would be sent to this school.

THE ROUSE COMMITTEE. The master reported that the "louse Committee bad left the arrangements to him to provide for the 10-11 annual trip to the seaside. The C3mmittee also pro- posed a hearty vote of thanks to Admiral Jones Parry for his gift of fruit trees to the Ilouse.—Mr. Norman moved the adoption of the report. He rsferred to the kindness of Admiral Parry in presenting to the houie a number of fruit tress, and proposed a hearty vote of thanks to him. This was seconded and carried unani- mously.

FINANCE COMMITTEE. Mr. Woodward reported that toe out-relief of the past fortnight had been Runcorn £9O; Frodsham £2B; Bod- worth £2l.—Mr. Meadowcroft called attention to the time of the meeting of the Finance Committee. It was impossible be said fer a member to attend this commit- tee if he was the member of another committee which met at the same time. Be censidered it was an unusual and unbueiaesseke course. Fer members to take the re- sponaibilite of attending the Finance and House Com- mittee and yet to h preeluded from the privilege of at- tending one was not in accord with his ideas, and par- ticularly as he proposed to take especial interest in the Anancial business of the Board. He considered it would be an advantage to have the House and Finance Committee meetings fixed at different hours. I only very reasonable propoeition, and if his suggestion wasn l ri 3 cared through, members would have privilege of attending the two meetings—Mr. Livaker endorsed all that Mr. Meadowcroft had said.— the Mr. Norman said this ma ter came before the committee of the House, and he vene9red the opinion neat the present arrangement had been made for the simple reason that they, could not pessibly have the meetings at different hours. There were eight or ten committees and to have them fixed at different hours would entiil considerable time. They would have to come there at nine o'clock, and would not be able to get away until five or six o'clock at night. By all the efoard being members of this Committee they could choose to attenc which ever they liked.—Mr. Woodward said it was Utterly impossible to make the hours of the different dommittees not t clesh. So far as he was concerned as as . Chairman of the Finapce Committee he would only be too pleased to bow to any arrangement for the eonvenience of the greater number of the Finance Committem.—The Chairman said this matter was thoroughly thrashed out in 1894,and several times since, but be did not see how they could improve their present arrangement.—Mr. Norman suggested that Mr. Meadowcroft should resige from one of the com- mittees.—Mr. Meadowcroft thought that he should not be called upon to throw over any priveledge he enjoyed simply because the House Committee did not see it con- venient to fix a suitable hour. He thought that after the appeal he had made to the Chairman of ,the House and Finance Committee aome disposition might ne made. If they went en the old rule they would never make any improvements.—The matter was then dropped and the committee's minutes were carried. THE CHAIRMEN OF COMMITTEES. Messrs. J. Mclntyre and S. Woodward were elected chairman and vice-chait man respectively of the Asses,- meat Committee. Messrs. S. Woodward and J. B. Chadwick, chairman and vice-chairman of the School Attendance Corrmittee. Messrs. J. Mclntyre and J. Weir, chairman and vice-chairman of the Parliamentary Committee. This was all the business.

div.head: CONSECRAIION OF -THE NEW CHURCH AT WESTON,
div.p: CONSECRAIION OF -THE NEW CHURCH AT WESTON,

For many years the need of a church has been felt throughout the village of Weston, but at last the long felt want has been supplied. Through the ardent and assiduous work of the incumbent of the parish of Runcorn, the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, M.A., and many willing co-workers there has been erected a beautiful church, and one that will in every way meet the requirements of the neighbour- , hood. The expenses for the building of the church have been raised by voluntary subscriptions ; but for the site the promoters are indebted to the Lord of the Manor (Major Orred), whose munificence within the parish is well-known. The sacred edifice occupies a commanding position in the centre of Weston, overlooking the Mersey and the Man- chester Ship Canal, in close proximity to the National Schools, and forms the principal of an ex- ceedingly prominent block—ranking as the first in the village. Beiefly' described, it is a compact, homely and comfortable buiPing, and Seems to be well provided with comforts for the worshippers in the way of seating, light, and 'heat, The exterior of the building is of native stone from the quarries of Messrs. Guest and C.., and although the tower is not quite completed its appearance is imposingly neat. There is no burial ground attached, but the space between the various buildings forming the group is filled out with grass plots interspersed' with the necessary gravel walks. The seating will accommodate 300 persons, and on special occasions room might be made for about 50 mare. On the whole, Weston and district is to be congratulated on the possession of such a bt ilding. On Wednesday afternoon the building was crowded and every available seat occupied, the occasion being that of the consecration of the building, which is to be called the " Cnurch of S. John the Evangelist." The Lord Bishop of Chester, ,(Dr. Jayne) performed the ceremony iwhich was a very impressive one, and was assisted b‘i his chap- lains, the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood (Runcorn) and the Rev H.B. Blogg (Frodsham),whilst Mr. Farmer, solicitor, Chester,acted as registrar. Before the con- elusion of the ceremony his lordship delivered an address from the pulpit founded on the worth " .magnify my office" Romans xi. 13, and "Look not every man upon his own things,but every man also upon the things of others " 2 Ephesians ii., 4. He sold his text should be taken in the aspect of a two-fold maxim, it did not mean that they were not to look after number one—they should do that in a reasonable manner—but it did mean they were to be unselfish and sympathetic. They must be considerate to others. Referring to the beautiful edifice they had succeeded in erect- ing, he asked, how many of the promoters, when they set out in their purpose of erecting a church for Weston ever hoped to,see such an one erected 'Surely. it waa beyond the most ambitious aspira- tions of even the most ardent of the church workers who had assisted so largely, and he could te-tify to the pleasure the duty was noon which he Was en- gage d ; but they must remember they Were not to become so engrossed flpotitheir own little church as to forget ethers, and whilst "magnifying their own office." they ehoukl still have regard for the things of others,and notierget the mother church. Special hymns were sung by an augmented surplice choir, in which the congregation joined heartily. In honour of the occasion there was a display of fireworks at night, end during the day the villaze was en fete with flags and bunting. is A correspondent oi the "Star" mentions the statement that Mr Chlinherkin, in order to divert his mind tem- porarily from the troubles with President Krueer ifl South Africa anci with the French in West Africa, which at the present moment must wieh on the mind of a Colonial Socretary, has written a play, the plot of whi...l is laid in the political world, which will be acted on private stages before strictly limited audiences. 14v Chamberlain was in his younor days a very clover amateur actor, and before he entered the HOll9O of COW- mons made a very fair hoginning as a play wriht in a drama which he entitled " Who's Who ? div.head: RUNCORN FOOTBfiLL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN FOOTBfiLL CLUB.
REVIEW OF THE PAST SEASON.

Football enth.isiests have now practically got over the excitement which is attendant on the doings of the clubs under the Northern Union. Their attention will now naturally he turned to sports more in keeping with the weather. Reverting to the d.nngs of the Runcorn Rugby fifteen during the past season it cannot be said that they in any way maintaimed the reputation which they so well earned two or three years ago when they distinguished themselves as the champions of the Lan- cashire section of the Nei.; hern Union. Never in the history of the club hat; it been known for them to be so backward in gaicing points as they heve been during the past season. The season 1896 and 97 ssw them near- ing the top of the ladder, and it MI5!: have indeed been surprising to football folks outside the Cheshire town to see the poor exhibitions week after week for at least ten or a dozen Saturdays this season, given by the once famous team. In the Cup Competitions in 1898 and 97 Runcorn fared very badly and particularly as far as the exchequer was concerned. The first two matches were with junior clubs and consequently tha gates were not as great as they would have undoubtedly been it two first class clubs had been pitted against each other. But as this mode of procedure was laid down by the superior authority we must abide by it. As far as the cup com- petitions and gate money were concerned this year,they proved to be an unqualified success. The " linnets " were pitted against Ulverston. a second class club, at Ulverston whom they easily accounted for. They gave the quietus to Brighouse R sneers lit the second time of asking. Oldham had also to work bard for honours against Runcorn in the third round and it was only Niter a tough struggle that they managed to check the Cheshire merle career. Hoerever, if they did not win the cup, they managed to achieve what I have al- ready mentione I, and what was perhaps the best under the circuiristaneee. It will enable the treasurer and other officials of the club to look with a hopeful view of the future, and when it is time for the " men of green " to enter the arena again, brighter hopes and aspirations will prevail. Whilst other teams have been augmenting their ranks with foreigners as it were, Runcorn and Warrington have remained steadfast to tradition. One thing seems peculiar and that is, that Runcorn appear not only to support their own team, but also others. For instance, Leigh have three Runcorniane in the persons of Moly- neux and the two Dunbavine, who have shone during the season, are looked upon in Leigh and district is the mainstays of that club. Turning nearer home the players were practically the same as those who did duty in the year 96 and 97. Butterworth is " the man," and the club at present would be nought without him. His , less was severely felt in the middle of the season when he was unable to play for some time swing to an injury. , Houghton at the back of the team is a veritable tower of strength, and minus him the team would be practi- cally without a defence. The notable additions to the I ranks have been the retern of Warder and the inclusion lof several new men, for instance Wilkinson, P. Abel, and W. E. Rough. The last named have been only on the teem for the latter part of thi season, and come- qut.ntly they have not been able to do much, but great ,thioga are expected of them next geese'''. !lough, who is still young, has been connected with football all his life. He commenced with a junior foot- ball club in the town of which Betterwor h and Houghton were also members. He then joined the Runcorn Association Club when it was in a flourishing way,and he highly delighted the officials con- nected with that club by his cleverness. He has played in almost every position on the Assecietion field, and for a few years was the full-back and also Captain. He has also splendid running powers,and his secession from the Association code to thet of the Rugby was hailed with great satisfaction by his many friends. Of course he wants practice to get him out of the Association way of playing foothill, and when he gets sufficient of that he will undoubtedly ba a valuable acquisition to the ranks of rugby football. Toe inter-works competition has also been a success from every point of view, and many of the participators in the games will no doubt be called upon in the coming season to do deity for their town. Before concluding this short sketch, I must refer to the lamentable death of Mr. James E.Langshaw, who had acted as the chief official, in the capacity of secretary to the club, for over 20 years. He had seen the club rise from that of a fourth rate position to that of champions. He unmistakably worked hard for the furtherance of the interests of the teams,and his untimely !:leath has been a great blow to the Northern Union and practically to the Runcorn club. rd r' and

div.p: SCALDED TO DETT d BY MOLTEN METAL

• A WIDNES FATALITY. Mr. S. Brighouse. coroner, held an inquest on Monday. ctamhef et vet darenFoafottahn atfatal f nt pitjjhue)rhineWsriiidnanyetoshei:Am.cmcaindoiuepnincitt.arlitto:o f some mol ten: Tues lay. He died on Fri.' day—Mr. J. vy. Knowles appeared to watch the. inter- ests of the Foundry Company,and Mr.Rowe,Government Inspector of Factories, was also prespnt.—Richard gaynes,father of the deceased ,gave evidence of identifi- cation.—Fraocis Brown stated that he had worked at the Widnes Foundry two years and sia months, and he I was a crane follower. Deceased, witness, and a man naraad Arthur Cawsey were all working together on the day in question. A ladle containing about seven tons of molten Metal was attached to a travelling crane, and was going through the process of skimming. Is order to do this one ,of . the catches on the bow side of the tulle had to be taken out. After the skimming bad bee. performed witness saw Cawsey put the catch back, and word was then given for the ladle to be hoisted no. Whew it had been hoisted about four feet it turned over and all the metal fell to the ground•As soon as witness observed the metal coming he ran out of the way, but he had •to jump into a tank of water to save himself. Be posi- tively swore that he saw Cawsey put the catch on.- -Arthur Cawsey corroborate :', and said it was his duty to skim the metal and also to put the catch back. Ques- tioned by the Coroner, he said that he had a very vivid recollection of turning the catch back. The pot (mean. lug tke ladle) had never been turned over before. It emptied completely.—Samuel Drought, foreman, said , he inspected the ladle after the accident had occurred, and he found the catches outwards. It did not follow when he found the catches outwards that they were in that position when the pot etarted to fall. When the ladle swung back they would naturally fait back. Wit- nett could not imagine the pot tilting over if both catches were • outwards. In witness's opinion it was very strange that the pot tilted at all.—When the catch had been removed it took some 13,3wer to pull it back.— Miss Warburton,matron, deposed to the deceased having suffered from burns about-the feet and other parts of the body, which resulted in death.—After the Coroner . had summed up. the jury returned' a verdict of" Aecideatal death." and were of the invinimous opiniou that de- ceased's dealt was CIUSf el by the citeh bne'sicle the bow of tLe ladle being off instead of on.

div.head: FATALITY AT HIGHFIELD TANNERY
div.p: FATALITY AT HIGHFIELD TANNERY
RUNCORN.

An accident ot a shocking nature occurred at the nightield Tannery, on Monday afternoon, when a young man named Archibald Hassell, one of the employees, sustained fearful injuries which termin- ated fatally about ieven o'clock the same evening At the time of the accident, it appears, that Has- sell was in the act of placing .a strap on the sham of some portion of the machinery, when he got caught in some unaccountable manner in the revolving whee Land before the machinery could be stopped,he got nipped by the strap and drawn into the pulley. When extracted it was found that his left toot had been taken clean off,and the other badly shattered., Dr. McLennan, and Dr. McDougall's aasistant were soon on the spot, followed shortly by the ambulance in charge of P.C. Carrington. The injured man having had his limbs attended to was then con- veyed to the railway station, and taken by the 3.40 express to Liverpool, where be was admitted to the Royal Infirmary. In spite of all that could be done for him he passed away after suffering great pain as above stated. Much sympathy is expressed on all hands at the yoang man's lamentable and sud- den end.

INQUE T. At the Liverpool Coroner's Court. yesterday, Mr. Ernest Gibson, deputy coroner for Liverpool. held an inquest concerning the death of Archibald Hassell, a labourer, 24 years of ago,wbo resided at 22,Notton-street Rancorn. Evidence was given by a foreman and labourers that it was a rule iu the works that the engine should be stopped before touching any belts. The Deputy Coroner said it appeared this nobody was to blame except the deceased himself, whe foolishly attempted the risky job of fixing the belt on a moving shaft. Mr. Sidney Brant, H.M. Factory Inspector, said a lot of accidents arose from the practice, and he wished some regulations could be framed to put a stop to it altogether. The jury decided that death was accidental, and recom - monied that thee, shoal he printedjootices in the works forbidding workmen touching the belting while the en- gine was working.

There was a fair attendance. SUDDEN DEATH cE A RESPECTED RESIDENT.—There passed away on Tuesday last, under somewhat tragic circumstances in the person of Mr. Peter Riley (foreman joiner at Messrs. Thomas D Ivies and Sons, builders), an old and respected resident of Frodsham. Mr. Riley's demise came as a great shock to the neighbourhood as for some time past he baa been enjoying the best of hethiand is not known to have suffered from anything beyond a slight attack of indigestion seine time ago. His end -was sudden and without any warning. He had only just left a few friends and proceeded a little way Jown the istreei.,when he was seen to fall,and expired almost on tbeinstsht.On.Wednesday night;at the Police Station, Mr. J. C, Bate (coroner) opened an Inquiry touching the cause'of death.—Evidence of identification was given by William Riley (the deceased's son). He said that he was with his father,who was 98 years of age, and other men In the Belle Monte Hotel, Overton, on the 107 h May at 8.30 a.m:, and remained there until 650 a.m. That was the last be saw of deceased alive ; he saw his father's dead body at aboUt 7.30 a.m. He never knew his father to suffer from anything save a slight attack of indiges- tion but that ivas some time past.—Thomas Ashworth, Marsh-lane,Frodsham,cated that about 7.30 on the 10th Mayo be was going down Main-street, Frodshans, and passed the deceased. When he had gone past be looked Mound and saw the deceased fall.He ran to him,but Riley expired after breathing a few times. He assisted in carrying deceased hesne.—lt not being considered neces- sary ta call medical evidence, after the coroner summed up,the jury retured cverdict of death from "natural causes." .

CONGREGATIONAL UNION. (Continued from Page 6). The proceedings were continued on Thursday. The businms ineuded the reading of a paper by Mr. A. Haworth, of Bowdon, en" The Suburban and City Pro bless : A Successful Experiment," in which the work of the Congregational Mission Board for Manchester, Sal- ford and the district was described.—The Chairmaa an- nounced that ha had rel,.-dved 4. letter from Htwar len. It was as follows :—" Miss Gladstone bags, oa behalf of M. Gladstone. to thauk tie ministers and dieega,:es of the Congregational Churches of England and Wales for their kind resolution of sympathy,and for their prayers." —The Rev. G. Campbell (Tollington Park) read a paper on "Th. Place of Evangelistic Mi.iiiollB in the w.)ric of the Churches."—Dr. Parker preached his usual weekly sermon. He extended a hearty welcome to the mem- bers of the Congregational Union, and said he was glad that accident had brought them to th 3 City Temple on that day. In the course of his sermon Dr. Parker impressed upon the congregation the duty of giving in the Master's service, not hecausn ha needeth their gifts —He could do without them—'out because He delighted in them, as they, after all, were, or ought to be, symbols of the extent of their love. Ths other day he heard in one of their own meetings one of their members announce that tney were endeavouring to raise the salary of some of their ministers from £BO to £9O. "God for- give them,";said the preacher, raising his hands hnplor- ingly, " for they know a-y:, what they do." To be compelled to make au effort to .do this was not worthy tof them.—A collection was made on behalf of the Church Aid Society.— In the evening the City Temple tess crowded whan the young people's demonstration was held. Mr. J. D. M'Clure, M.A., L.L.D. Olin Hill), presided, sad on the platform were a large number of the leaders of Noncon- formity. Addresse.s were delivered by the chairman Rev. J. H. Jove,et (Birmingham), and the Rev. C Silver • ter Horns (Kenaington), and, during the evening a pri gramme of vocal music wed rendered.

ASSAULT AND BAD LANGI:TAGN,

On Friday before Alderman Harrison (in the chair), Councillor H. Roberts. Councillor James Smethurst. Mr. James Hepherd, nod Dr. Gornall. In this ease the com- plainant John Forster, 9, Galewarth-street, summoned Mrs. Hannah Ogden, for assault on the 27th April. Mr. Forshaw appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Browne for the defendant. The complainant was in the employ of Mr. W. D. Houghton and Sons. He said ca the 27th of April, he was coming home from work, and Mrs. Og- den met him and assumed a very threatening attitude, win some bad language to him. Be asked her what was the matter and she struck him in the face. She afterwards saw his wife, seized her by the throat, and nearly choked her. Mr. Brown cress-examined the complainant. William Patin was called for the prosecu- tion. Be saw the defendant strike compluinant in the face on the day in question. Ernest Seed a youth, who worked at W. D. Houghton and Sons was called as a witless for the defence. Mr. Browne said on the face of the evidence given, the complainant (John Forster) must lave done something to her or she would not have used the bad language. She denied having struck him at all. The defendant, the wife of George Ogden, a blind man, said the complainant's wife on Tuesday night challenged her te come out, after she had done a bard day's washing. When she met Forster ne C her and she pushed him.fle said to her he would knock her husband up and down the street but for him being blind. Susannan Smith was called for the defence. The bench imposed a fine of Si and costs or a week's im- prisonment.

At the Warrington Borritigh Police Court on Tuesday, before Mr.flobert Garnett(in the chair)and other !nava- trate, William Salt, 32, Cartwright-street, was charged witlocrommitting on aggravated assault upon his wife Maria Salt on Monday Afternoon. Toe prisoner was ' formerly landlord ef the Shakespeare Inn, Dolman's-lane. —Maria Salt, his wife, said, before going out yesterday she told him she was going to complain of his cooduct to the police. He had been drinking and his cooduct had been very bad to her lately. She had heen supporting him since January. After coming back he asked bee if sue had complained to the police. She said abs had done so. He then struck her twice at the hack of the head. She then picked up a glass to throw at him. but he struck her before she could throw it at him. He said he would bang for her. In going from his further violence she fell upon her knees. Prisoner had not worked since Clstrnas.--Elizabeth Salt, a daughter, about fourteen years of age, corroberated her mother's evidenee. She was in the house at the time her mother came back after telling the police of her father's conduct, She saw her father strike her mother.—Sergeant Bell said in conse- quence of a reoort being brought to the police 'natio° th-t the man William Salt had been attempting to mur- der his wife, he went to Cartwright-street. The house looked as if a struggle had taken place in it. It was upset and there was a lot of broken crockery a''out. Mn. Salt as brought to the Police Station in a cab. She had a bandage on her bead.He took:the man William Solt into custody. The prisoner was under the influ- ence of drink. He said " Take me away and give me twelve months "—The prisoner when asked to make his statement said "I have had no peace with the woman ever since I came out of work." Be admitted he had had drink. He said be naked her if she had told the police as she had threatened to have him turned out of house. That was how it began. She had broken elegises on his head Life had been a hell with her this lest few weeks.—The Bench lined him 406. and costs for in default, one menth's imprieonment. The wife then applied for a separation order with the custody of the I children. The Beech made the order out for her hus- band to pay her 102. per week, and granted her the custody of the children. THY, CONGREGATIONAL UNION,

The 66th Annual Assembly of the Congregations. Union of England and Wales began its proceedings on Monday night at the Memorial Hall, Farringdon-street, London,the Rev. A. Rowland,the chairman of the Union presiding. There was a crowded attendance of ministers and delegates. The committee's report, which was adopted,rererred, among other timings, to the treatment of the Bechuanas aud a correspondent on the subject with Sir Gordon Sprigg and Sir J. Sivewright, to whom a pretest was sent bo the committee against the practi- cal enslavement of the people. The ballot for the chair- manship of the Union for 1899 ended in favour of the Rev. H. Arnold Tnomas,of Bristol. On the motion of the Rev. Dr. Mackennal,a resolution was passed in favour of Sunday closing of licensed houses in England and ea- pressin; sympathy with the action of magistrates who had directed the holders of off-licenses not to supply intoxisatin,g drinks to children under thirteen years old.

The proceedings were centinued on Tuesday. The presidential address was given by the Rev. A. Rowland, who spoke on the : object of united action on the Free Churches. The Rev. Dr. P. S. MOXDITI received a cordial welcome as a delegate representing the Congregation. lists of the United States. He said that the heart of the States was sound in its sympathy with Eugland. The two branches of the Anglo-Saxon race should draw together in the great enterprise of the world's evangelisa- tion and the world's education. He knew of no such august possibilities lying before any race as lay before the Anglo-Saxon race along the lines of progressive and pacific civilisation. The time had come when nations thinking alike en the great moral problems of our time must clasp hands and stand shoulder to shoulder. A resolution of sympathy with America in the war was carried. A resolution was adopted protesting against the continued alliance of Church and State in this country, and expressing streng disapproval of the proposed endowireut from State finds of a Roman Catholic University in Ireland. A resolution expressing symphathv o ith Mr. Gladstone was also included in the day's proceedings. The proceedings in connection with the sittings of the Congregational Union of England and Wales were con- tinued on Wedoesday in London. A large congregation assembled in the City Temple in the morning, when the Rev. J. M. Gibbon, of Stamford Hill, preached the annual sermon for the London Missionary Society. The rev. gentleman took for his text St. Luke xxiv., 41 —" They yet believed not for joy, aud wondered." The sixth annual meeting of the Watchers' Band, an off- shoot of the London Missionary Society, was held in the afternoon, under the presidency of the Rev. Alfred Row- land. chairman of the Congregational Union. The re- port stated that the Band had made steady growth dur- ing the past year. In the home division forty-four new branches have been registered, making a total in this division of 665. The new members number 2,954, mak- ing a total enrolled 26,878. The number of branches in all the divisions is 768, and the number of members en- rolled 29,378. compared with 714 branches and 26,869 members reported last year.—The annual public meeting of the London Missionary Society took place on Wednes- day evening in the Queen's flail, Langharn-place, under the chairmanship ot Mr. Evan Spicer J.P. The prin- cipal object of the meeting was to welcome the foreign secretary (the Rev. R. Wardlaw Thompson) on his re- turn front his journey round the world, dur- ing which he visited the mission fields where the society's work was being ej carried eon.— The Rev. Wardlow Thompson was loudly cheered as he rose to make his report. He gave an interesting ac- count of his 50,000 miles of travel. Alluding NI Mada- gascar, he said there were signs every where that the hands of the French soldiery had been laid on the land. Many of the free churches had been used by the soldiery for secular purposes. It was, indeed, a pitiable mani- festation of anti-English feeling. He believed that the deputation had proved to the general in command that the missionaries were not spies in the pay of the English Government, aud that the French Government honestly intended to give the society the same fair play which it gave to other people in Madagascar. (Cheers.) He must however, say that their Mssion would never be in the same position again as it had been. It had lost prestige as being the church of the aristocracy. Catholicient would now be the fashienable religion among the multi- tudes of that country.—During the evening presonta- Mons of beautifully-bound volumes dealing with South Sea mission work,wewe made on behalf of the directors of the society to Mr. W. Croslield, J.P. (Liverpool),and Mr. Evsn Spicer ia recognition of their services in accom- panying Mr. Wardlaw Thompson in his journey.

div.head: VITELIIIS LOSC-HIS APPEME.
div.p: VITELIIIS LOSC-HIS APPEME.

" Vita Hue," says the historian, " lost his appetite." And small blame to him. Any man might well have done the same under the circumstances. Far Vitolius was a politician depending for both his prosperity and his life upon the favour of Nero. And the f IVMUr of that eminent statesman Was ever an uncertain quality. He was a " boss"—as the Americans put it—of a most despotic and overbearing character. What he would do was hard to divine; yet that he would de something mean and wieked was fairly sure. To oppose him was a bid for humediate destruction ; to serve him was only a trifle safer. This feet, as may be imagined, made an official career under Nero a very ticklish and worrying business.

Within a few days previous to the date to which the historian refers several courtiers had received intimation rum the Enap Tor that he would thereafter try to ran the Government without their help ; and also that it miglat save them further touble if they should at once "open their veins "; in other words, kill themselves. The effect of this hint upon the different persons concerned is described; "and, as for Vitelius," it is deliciously sug- gested, "he lost his appetite." We can easily believe it, especially when we tremens- bar that, under the ("mikes, orders of that sort always went for their face value. If the man couldn't run sway —which was difficult—he had to commit suicide. eh I dear rue. If nothing less than an incident such as happened to this Roman patrician could spoil one's appetite what lucky dogs we should be 1 Bat almost any mental shock or disturbance will npset the appetite; and than we shouldn't try to eat. Long continued, an Impaired appetite NCH produce indigestion, just as indi- gestion, when it oocurs first, will ruin Ihe appetite. The two play into each other's hands. But, bear in mind when the appetite is below par it is worse than useleei trying to force matters. I read a pamphlet the other day (a kind of advertising pamphlet I think it was) in which the writer said we should not tolerate any dis- position on the part of the stomach to shirk its duty ; if it doesn't call for food we ought to till it full anyway, Sv., &a. This is a mistake. On his own theory that man should try to cure a grained ankle by dancing a hornpipe on it, or an inflamed eye by compelling it to read a thousand pages of line print. Bah ! the idea is erroneous, and will not bear the light of day. When Mr. George Newman los', his appetite he didn't stuff himself with food to spite his stomach. He knew better. He looked around for a medicine to cure the disease that caused it, and (eventually) he found one.

" For many years," be sap, I suffered front bron- chitis. I was so low and weak it was bard for me to get about. My appetite was bad, and even the little I ate gave me pain at the chest and aLosnach. I was terribly troubled with phlegm, and continually straining to bring it up. My breathing was laboured, and often I could scarcely get my breath. During the summer I got on fairly well, but every winter I had very bad attacirs,and was confined to the house for weeks. I was unable to follow any regular employment, and at the best could only work a little at a time on my allot- ment.

" Year after year I suffered ; sometimes so badly I thought my time had come. In January of this year (1897), Mr. Simpson, of this parish, told me of the good Mother Seigel's Syrup had done him, and persuaded me to try it. He gave me a bottle,and after I bad taken it I felt myself another man. I could eat and enjoy my meals,and was in every way easier and better. I get a further supply from Mr. Goody„Chemist, and continued taking it. Soon my breathing was quite easy and na- tural ; the pains left me and I grew stronger. By tak- ing a little now and then I keep in good health. You may publish this statement as you like."—(Signed) Geo. Newman, Belch:imp St. Paul Clare, Suffolk, November 12, 1897. Appetite is Nature's way of letting you know that she needs focd and can digest a reasonable amount of it. When there is no appetite (or hunger) either the body has food enough for the present or the digestive organs are diseased and can dispose of little or none even if rt calved. The latter was Mr. Newman's condition. He had dyspepsia; his stomach could not handle food pro_ perly, and Nature notified him of it by spoiling his appe- tite and by punishing him with pain for every mouthful he swallowed. Yet to live, he was obliged to eat! A miserable and a dan7erous state of things. Happily Mother Seigel's Sera', solved the contradictory problem by curing his dyspepsia. Vl:aline, as we have learned, lost his appetite through fright and: fear. No medicine could help hint. His only remedy was to gat out of Ner.a's clutches. When appetite ceases from mental reasons, shake them off as soon as you can. But when the cause is indigestion or dyspepsia—the common cause—the cure is at your finger's ends—Take Mother Seigel's Syrup.

The weather was most unpropitious, and militated against large congregations in the early part of the day. Special hymns were sung by the children at both morning and evening services, and at the latter, solos were rendered by Miss E. Gutteridge and Master Laithwaite. At the morning service the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. E. St. A. Duke, vicar of St. Dunstan's, Liverpool, and in the even- log by the Rev. J. Davies, vicar of St.. Anne's, War- rington, both of whom preached appropriate sermons. In the afternoon, an organ recital was given by Mr E. Leyland, organist, with musical selections by the choir, but there was only a very poor audience. The programme, which was very well rendered, was as follows :—Organ" Barcarole from 4th Concerto " ; solo," The garden of prayer", Miss Nellie Gorse; organ, " Fanfare "; chorm, " As pants the hart " ; solo, " The voice of the Father" Mr. W. This Council met in the Board Room at Great Sankey Board Sohools on Monday evening. Mr. Joseph Wright occupied the chair and there were also present : —Mr. William Thompson, Mr. William Taylor, Mr. T. Cooke,with Mr. smith (clerk). THE CHAIRMAN RETURNS TRANX.S. Mr. Wright on taking the chair, thanked the members for the honour conferred upon him at the last meeting by electing him a 9 chairman of the Council.lle hoped they might all work amicably to- gether, and at the end of twelve months they might have benefitted the township without having raised the rates.

THE MORTUARY QUESTION. . The Clerk stated that he wrote to the secretary of the Local Government Board with reference to the powers of the Council to rent a room for mortuary purposes. The letter had been acknowledeed,but no further communi- cation had been received.—The Chairman said it was very important that something should be done. He understood that the last body found in the township was kept at Mr.llnsworth's place from Monday until the following Saturday.—The Clerk said he had had a con- versation with the police on the matter and he was informed that the delay in burying the body was in con- sequence of one of the relatives of the deceased having taken over the responsibility, and then neglecting to do his duty in the matter.—Mr. Cooke said he was given the same explanation.—lt was decided to adjourn the matter until the next meeting. PROPOSED BALLOTING AT PARISH annerixos. A communication was read from the Ewhurst Parish Council suggesting various amendments with regard to secrecy of voting by electors at the Parish meeting and suggesting a ballot instead of the present mode of voting; thus preventing people from voting for more than the proper number of candidates, and giving more liberty to the electors to exercise their own judgment.—On the proposition of Mr. William Thompson, seconded by Mr. Taylor, it was decided that the Clerk should write sup- porting the resolution of the Ewhurst Council. • BOX FOR DOCIINDINTS. After some discussion it was decided on the proposi- tion of Mr.Cooke,secondel by Mr.Taylor,that the Chair- man and the Clerk eh-mid purchase a box in which the Clerk could preserve Parish documents. TEE DOST OS THE PARISH COUNCIL ELECTION. The Clerk stated that he had received an from Mr. Sutton, the returning officer, for the i'arish Council election. The account was for ES I.' was a little less than the preceding one, w' LS 174. id. This was a little less than a ..„,eeing one,which was for £.3 158. 91.—A cheque WM Signed for • that amount. TRH MEETINGS OF THE corfrerr,. Mr. Thompson moved that the meetings of :he Coun- cil be held quarterly, th 3 dates to be fixed by the Ccuncil. He thought that number of meetings would be sufficient to enable them to transact the business of the Council. If there was any special business, meetings could be called in addition.—Mr, Cooke seconded ,and it was agreed to unanimously. It was also decided that the meetings should be held as near quarter day as possible. This concluded the business. .. .oise ' WARRINGToeI FOOTBALL CLUB WOHXB COMPETITION.

In connection with the ab3ve competition the following sums have been handed over to the local institutions :—The Infirmary, £45 ; the Nurses' In- stitution, £l5; and the St. John Ambulance, £3 10s. SHARP-IMM PRIMITITE METEOR= CHAPEL. The third Sunday school Anniversary Sermons in connection with this prosperous institution were held on Sunday. The scholars assembled in the Mission at 9 a.m , and after an opening ceremony formed into procession, headed by the superinten- dents and teachers, and perambulated the neigh- bouring streets, notwithstanding the unpropitious . weather. They sang at intervals special and ap- propriate anniversary music, which was greatly appreciated by the people en route. At 11 o'clock a return was made to the mission when a very en- ouraging address was delivered to teachers,scholars parents, and friends, by Mr. J. Whitley, Stockton Reath. At 1.30 the scholars paraded the thorough- fares repeating the music of the morning. In the afternoon and evening the Rev. W. J. Kirirland, Birmingham (Ist circuit) preached to crowded congregations two most inspiricg and eloquent sermons, characterised by the same earnestness, energy and vigour, which marked this gentleman's former ministry in this town. The singing by adult and juvenile choirs, under the leadership of Mr. Butterfield, was of a very high order, and con- stituted a special feature of the services. The au. thems rendered were Praise ye the Lord," and "The Earth is the Lord's," the soloi being taken by Miss Bridge and Mr J Knowles. in a style most creditable to both. Miss Butter- worth (Manchester), wae exceedingly impressive in her solos" Beyond the Gate " and the' Children's Children's Rome " fully justifying the reputation she has WOO at the Manchester concerts. On Monday even- ing a congregational tea was held followed by Mr. irrilliatnivde Methodism"'spopula popular lecture entitled " Heroism in which proved hignly interes- ting and instructive. The chair was occupied by Mr. J.Grifsiths. The hartnoniumists were Mr. J. W. Travis (Warrington) ,and M r. T. S. Bridge (Burn- ley), to whom a large share of the musical success is due. The collections exceeded those of previous years, realising over £l2.

div.head: BANNER.
div.p: BANNER.

Some short time ago a sale of work was held in connection with the Wesleyan body of Earlestown, for the purpose of getting together funds for the purchase of a new banner to be used during school processions. The sale was an unqualified success, and the Committee in charge of the matter were enabled to place an order for a new silk banner, with Messrs. Tootill of London. The banner having arrived, opportunity was taken of a visit of Mr. John Barr, formerly a superintendent of the Sunday School, and now of Southport, to unfurl it. A. meeting was held in the Wesleyan Lecture Hall on Monday evening when there was a numerous gathering, presided over by the Rev. P. R. pus. more. Addrrsees were delivered by past and pre- sent Superintendents of the Sunday School, includ- ing Messrs. J. Roberts, G. Howarth, J. Mitchell, J. H. Profit, W. Pearson, W. Clare, G. Burgess. &.e._ Mr. Barr. in unfurling the banner, said as the National flag of our country spurred us on to vic- tory, so let that banner be an incentive to them to progress in the good work. Vocal selections were given during the evening by Miss M. Barr and Miss M. Clare, Miss K. Chandley presiding at the piano. The banner, which is entirely of silk; has cost some- lhing like 1"25, and is of a beautiful design. On the front is the figure of Christ sowing' the seed, surmounted by the name of the Sunday School,and on the reverse aide is Christ as the Good Shep- herd. It is expected it will be used for the first time on Whit Monday. A:4 Horß or EonLxsxossrfe TAMA 1.0.G.T. The first weekly meeting of the new quarter was held in the Co-operative Hall on Monday night, when C.T. Bro. J. Taylor presided. A good attend- ance was present, and the installation was gone through. Different matters arose with reierence to the programme for the quarter, and various com- mittees were appointed. One candidate was ad- mitted to the Order, and Bro. E. Newman gave the report of the Convention held at Ashton on Satur- day last, and stated that the next place of meeting will be at Warrington. Bro. J. Woods afterwards gave further details of it. Arrangements were then made for the pic-nic, and after other business the Lodge closed.—On Tuesday evening the above Lodge visited the Primitive CE, and under the presidency of Bro, T. Cutler, a successful gather- io present. After the singing of a second the Chairman based a few remarks on the l'ernnerance Cause" and said that it was their object to leave the world better than they found it, Sister Hill then rendered a song in a pleasing way, followed by a reading from Bro. E. Newman, after which Sister A. Owen rendered " head kindly light "in a satisfactory way. Sister R. Warburton pleased the audience with "The Avon," followed by a reading from Bro. Cutler ; afterwards Bro. Hobbs giving two selections on the dulcimer. -Mrs. Oode then rendered a song, and Bro. Wilson a mouth organ solo, followed by a recitation by Sister R. Warburton. Sister Maud Walton excel- lently rendered" Send forth Thy Love," a recita- tion afterwards being given by Sister Gerrard. Mr. Rawlins said the C.E. were very much indebted to the Hope of Earlpstown Lodge for the excellent programme they had given, • and thanks were accorded to the visitors. Bro. W. Willis proved an efficient accompanist, and the meeting ended with the Benediction being pronounced • hr, Bro. J. Woods.

Mn. H. W. SBTON KARR FOR SOMALILAND. Mr. W. H. Seton-Kart, of Atherton Grange, %Vim bledon, the well-known explorer and sportsman has just accepted an invitation ftom Dr. Lunn, to take charge of a lion and rhinoceros hunting'. ex- Pedition to Somaliland in the autumn. Mr. Seton Karr, the Due d'Orleans, Lord Delamere, Sir tfenry Tich borne. and other well-known sportsmen, have I found Somaliland the finest huntinq gronnd in the 'world. Lord Delatnere has bagged upwards oF fifty lions in his various expe4ition-.and Mr. Sston-Karr's record is only Second to his. Mr. Seton-Karr is also an enthusiastic archeologist, and has recently brought back from what he claims to be the cradle of the human race and the probable site of the Garden of Eden, paleolithic imolements which hare been purchased by the British Museum and other institutions for upward 3 of Ma It is expected that a number of scientists as well as sportsmen will visit this part of Somaliland. div.head: PRINCE OF WALES'S LANCASHIRE VCSIT.
div.p: THE PRINCE OF WALES'S LAN- CASHIRE VCSIT.

OFFICIAL PROGRAMME. All the arrangr-rneets connected with the visit of the Priace of Wales to Garswood Flail (Lord Gerard's Lan- cashire seat) and Southport.are now complete, and al- though the primary object of the visit is to be present at the review of the Lancashire I3ussars, several other functions have been added to the programme. Accom- panied by Sir Evelyn Wood and other officers, His Royal Highness will arrive at Newton-'e-Willows Station (Lon- don and Nerth-Western) about six o'clock ea the even- ing of Tuesday the 17th inst. Carriages will be waiting, and the party will be driven direct to Gars wood Hall, entering the park by the lodge on the flaydock side of Asht,in-in-Makerfield. On the Wednesday morning His Royal Highness and suite will drive to Bryn Station,and thence travel by special train over tho Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway through Wigan to Southportorrivine at Chapel-street Station at 10.45. Here the Mayor of Sauthport (Alderman S. L. Booth) will present an ad- dress of welci-me, after which His Royal Highness will host) the inearb irs of the 3rd R., woo will be drawn up in the station as a guard of 'amour. Then the Prince and his party will mount hnrses to readiness in the station yard and ride on to the Birkd 'le Sands by way of London-street, Nevill-street, and the Promenade. After the review of the Hussars, of which Lord Gerard is the commanding officer, His Royal Highness will return into Southport by the same route and make a grim, stoppage at the Victoria Hotel,the headquarters of the regiment. From the hotel the Prince will proceed in a carriage to the Municipal Buildings by way of the promenade, Saabank-ro ad (passing the Convalescent Hospital), and Lord-street. In the Art Gallery a. recep- tion will be Wild, followed by a luncheon in the Cam- bride Hall, at which the members of the Town Council and their wives and the officers of the regiment and their gueste will be present. There is 0 be no speech- making. The Prince will be asked by the Mayor to plant a tree in front of the Town Hall in commemoration of his visit, and then he will drive by way of Eastbank— street, and Chapel-street to the station,and go by special train to Wigan, arriving at 4.15. An address will be presented by the Mayor on behalf of the Corporation,and from the station the Prince will drive out of the town by way of Wallgate, Caroline-street, and Chapel-lane,and MR to Garswood Hall. Ho will return to Leadon on Thursday morning, taking the train at Newton-le-Wil- lows.

THE ARRANGEMENT' OP Tag NsvvroN COUNCTL. At the tn-seting of the Urban District C ouncil held at th Town Ball. Earlestown, on Monday afternoon. several resolutions were EN bmittmi for confirm .tion by the G.meral Purposes Committee dealing with the arrangements proposed to he carried into eff,ct on the occasion of the paasing of H.R.R. the Prince of Wales through Newton-le•Willows when visiting Lord Gerard at Garswood Mall. At the meeting of the General Pur- poses Committee en April 11th, it was resolved that Mr. Wood he requested ta ask Lori Gerard if he would he good enough to ascertain whether his Royal Highneaa the Pt ince of Wales would be pleased to receive an address of welcome frone the members of the Council on hie arrival at Newton-le-Willows station on the 17th of My. The Clerk was also instructed to write to the Local Government Board requesting their sanction to the expenditure by the Council of a reason- ahle sum of money on the presentation of an address to FI.R.M. the Prince of Wales, and on the display of much bunting ac miLlht be thought necessary.—At a further mseting of the Committee held oh Welnesdsv, April 27th, Mr. Wood stated that he had received a letter from Lord Gerard, informing, him that H.R. a. the Prince of Wales would receive an address from the Council upon his arrival at Newton-le-Willows Station, on the _

I:7t-h -.M.t.y7 1393, but it en.USt—be—simplY handed in and the reply the same, whereupon it was resolved that an address he presented to H.R.H. the Prince of Wales, on the 17th day of May, 1893 —The Clerk react a draft of an address, which, after amend- ment was agreed to. I.; was or derel that the Clerk be authorised to spend a sum not exceeding 210 on the ad- dress which was suggested ehould be in album form and enclosed in a case. The address to be photographed be- fore presentation,—lt was further resolved that the Chairman, Dr. Patterson, Messrs. Simpson, McMahon, Gilmour, and Beatty, be a sub-committee to make and carry out arrangements for the display of bunting,which was B:l!Zeated should be done at the expense of the Council,in Church-street Newton.leaving it to the inha- bitants to decorate farther if desire-I —ln moving the confirmation of the soinutes,Mr.Smon Raid he had been told that des" that His Royal Highness would arrive at Newton-le-Willows about 8.30 o'clock on the 17th Inst. The Prince of Wales had expreseed his willingness to receive an address and he (Mr. Barron) hoped that every member of the Coun- cil would be able to attend. He believed Mr. Ward had arranged for a proper and reasonable reception of His Royal Highness. A good committee had been appointed to superintend the decorations which he was certain wield be carried nut to the satisfaction of the Council. —Mr. MeMehon seconded the confirmation of the minutes, which were unanimously agreed to. 'Pp, arrangements in nonnnectices with the arrival of FI.R.FI. the Prince of Wales at Newton le-Willews on Thursday evening next en route to Garswood Hall, are in a forward state. A meeting between the committee of the Council who have the arrangements in hand. Mr. Shaw and Mr. Andrewa of the London and North Weston Railway Company took plane at Newton on Monday. It has been arranged that H.R.R. after leaving the station shall proceed by a temporary covered way to his carri- age which will be drawn lip alongside a temporary platfnrm in Mill-lane, near the Railway Arches. Here he will be received by the District Council a,nd presented with ao address of welcome, but there will be no speak- ing. The C smmittee have been empowered to spend a sum not exceeding £2O in decorations about the station approaches, and on the line of !mute as far as the Oak Tree Inn. Crow-lane. The Newton Company of the Bth will furnish the guard of honour, and the route, as far as the Ashton boundary will be kept by 70 police, with 7 mounted constables, all under the charge of Superintendent Fligginhottom. The side streets lead- ing on to Highatreet,will be barricaded by the Council. Prom the Ashton boundary thp route will be kept by members ef the Wigan County Pollee. His Royal High- ness will leave London at 2 o'clock. and will travel be special train to Newton where he will arrive at 8.30 p.m. After performing the ceremonies he is announced to per- form at Southoort, he will return to London, leaving Newton at 2.30 on Thursday.

div.head: NEWTON DIVISION CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION. -- TFIE HON. T. W. LEGFI._ M.P., ON FOREIGN
div.p: NEWTON DIVISION CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION. -- TFIE HON. T. W. LEGFI._ M.P., ON FOREIGN

AFFAIRS. The annual meeting of the above Association was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Saturday afternoen,when there was a large attendance ef deleeates from all parts of the division. Mr. T. D. Grlmke Drayton presided. Mr. Helfand Owen (hon. secretary) read the annual report of the Council in which they recorded with deepest regret the loss the Association had sustained through the deaths of Mr. Marcus Brown-Westhead, and Mr. Thomas Stone, and desired to testify to the great services they had rendered the cause. The report else referred to the loss sustained by the death of Mr. William Royston, late vice-chairman of the Warrington Polling district, and recorded coatinuld confi lence in the hon. T. W. Legh, and desired to thank him for his careful attention and untiring energy in watching the interests of the cause generally. (Applause). Mr. R Stone, hon. treasurer, slid the statement of accounts for the past year was most satisfactory, the total cost of working the association being is 4d, less than in ISM, so that t ) '57 would see they had practised some little economy.—The reports were adopted on the motion of the chairman.—The Chairman moved that the best thanks of the members of the Association be given to Lord Gerard, and that he he re-elected Presi- dent of the asociation.—Mr. W. Valiant seconded, and the motion was unanimously carried. On the motion of Mr. Collinowood,seconded by Mr.W. R. Owen,Messrs, Voisey, Worthington, and Barton were reappointed hon. auditors.—Dr. Handyside and Mr. C. B.F. Borron were appointed representatives to the Lan- cashire and Cheshire Union of Conservatives. Mr. C. F. Clark moved, "That this meeting of the members of the Newton Division Conservative Associa- tion desire to accord their unabated confidence in her Majesty's Government, being fully convinced that its foreign, colonial, and domestic policy is calculated to promote the best interests of the British Empire." Mr. Catterall seconded the motion.

The Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P., supported the resolution. After referring to the dernestic legislation of the Government and to the Spanish-American war, he dealt at some length with the situation in the Par East. He said that this subject.clespite expressions to the contrary from Lord Salisbury and others, was the least satisfac- tory of those which called for consideration at the pre- pia ryt time. It happened that there were British ships at Port Arthur at the time when the Russian aggressive movement was perfectly plain. The Russians represented that the presence of British ships there was an unfriendly act. We had a perfect right to on there, but the Russian Ambassador came to I..c.rd Salisbury and asked him to take the ships away. Lord Salisbury said that he did not order the ships away, and doubtless he did not, but somehow or other they came away. That certainly had a most unfortunate result because the Rus- sian Minister in Pekin obviously went to the Chinese Government and said"We have ordered the British ships out of Port Arthur ;" and the Chinese believed it. To be perfectly honest, he Inuit admit that if this incident had happened when Lord Rosebery was in office the Union- ists would have made a great deal of it. After this had occurred, It was suggested that we should lend the Chinese money. The Chinese wonld have been only too thankful to take money from us, but here again the Russians stepped in and absolutely forbade the loan. Then, at length, all disguises were abandoned,the mask was thrown off.and the Russians came to us and calmly told us in polite language that they had not been speak- ing the truth all the time, and that they had always in- tended to occupy Port Arthur. It was then impossible for us to turn them one—things had gone too far. We were therefore obliged in self-defence to take the step of

, occupying tVei-Ilai-Wei. Failing anything else, we had taken, this pia,m ; and he. bail no doubt that, for strate- gical reasora,, G wernm mt were perfectly rif..; it in going there. (Gear, bear:) Lord Salisbury, who af4er all was the 'person whobe opinion ought to be best worth ' having, asserted that we hail gained and that tho Rus• slang had lost. He (Mr. -igh) was afraid, although be was only a humble member of the, party, that he did' not i quite look at it in this -light, and ho .was ' not quite -sure that the country. would look at it in this light either. (i voice: Bear, hear') The Russians had also establishedtherntieluee at Ta. Le- n place which We asked for and did not get, but which they took without asking. They. werein posses- sion of the whole of Manchuria, and could bring troops quite close to.Pekin,. Great.Britaln, on the other band, for offences and strategical purposes load only got Wei- Hai-Wei, we had obt dried exoellenr concessions, on paper,and if the Chinese adhered te theW bargain British trademo doubt, would profit by them. Sc:il!, he was cot quite satisfied in his own mind,despite what Lord SIRS bury said, that we had got the best of the bargain., -He was not so presumptuous, of course,as to set his opinion against that of Lord Salisbury and the -Government.. He was simply expressing the do ibtA watch occurred to him,and doubts which he thought wero fcltrattier widely' in the country. In conclusion, Mr. Legh acknowlsdged the fairness and restraint ehown by the responsible Opposition towards the Government during the recent negotiations. . S. _

The resolution was further supported by Mr. R. pit_ kington, mayor of St. Helens, and adoptod. A vote of thanks to this Hon. T. W. I,,gh for his ser- vices, and an expression of confidence in him, concluded the meeting.
NOT liB aANIES AND • ATHLETICS.

The visit of our local let eleven to Blackley on Satur- day was attended with defeat. Datil this season the Blackleyites have not neon coosidered quite the class of Warrington, but their performances last year justified them in getting fixtures with clubs of better standing this season. The result to them has been satisfac- tory. With us it is the reverse. The captain, Dr. R.t Smith, was absent from the VVarrington ranks. There were a fair number of appreciative spectators on the well apportioned ground.

The visitors won the toss, and J. Callon and Tnewlis were opposed by Ashton and Turner. A disastrous start was made on the slow wicket, for from Turner's fourth. ball Callon failed to get a thorough hold and was easily taken at Mid-on. Disaster did not end there, for with three added Clarke in playing forward to Ashton failed to get back, and Phillips' smartness was responsible for the seacind wicket.

When Connor joined Thawlis a short stand was made. The professional nit Turner to the boundry, wnilst Con- nor turned his attention to Ash^oa, hittin.z. him for three fours in quick succession. Twenty was hoisted, hut at this total a double disaster befel the visitors. Thewlis being got in taro minds, whilst without any addition Connor was bowled. W. H. Podmore, and J. W. Bibby looked like staying the" rat," a brilliant hit past paint by Podmore being loudly applauded. At 33. however, Podmore was bowled, whits; Voisey three runs later skied one to Pickering. .

• --- Bowen joined his captain, and runs came very freely. Fifty was soon sent up, eacti batsman playing the bowl- ing with cAafideace. 'Chia partnership was responsible for 32 runs before Bowen was bowled for a useful 18. whilst two runs later Bibby was taken by Hanson off Boardman, that player having just relieved Ashton. Elarnpson and Morgan gave trouble, the last-named quickly putting together 14, and the innings closed for 811

Blackley started their essay with A. G. Wood and Hanson, the bowling being started by Thewlis and Con- nor. A confident appeal by Thewlis for Hanson lbw was ruled in favour of trio batsman, whilst at eight the Warrington professional again appealed for Hanson, without success. A brilliant catch by Hampson sent Wood back at eight, and Baardman joined llansoci.Runs came at long intervals, the fielding of the visitors being excellent, and twenty was hoisted after half-an-hour's play.

Bibby relieved Connor, and Podmore was tried in place of Thewlis at 40, and the last change at once proved effective, for Boardman failed to resist the tempting slows from Podmore, and Callon brought off a fine catch. Hood joined Hansen, who began to score rapidly, and though the original bowlers resumed it was not until the total had reachod 74 that a change was effected.

Clarke relieved Connor, and the new bowler at once met with remarkable success. Off his first ball Hanson was caught at cover point, and alter Thewlis had been responsible for the dismissal of Ashton, Clarke in quick succession sent back Mood, Hibbert, and Maddick, the wickets being hit in each instance, and seven wickets wore down far 83 runs. Pickering and Midwood, ever. soon placed the issue beyond doubt, and the winning hit was made by Mid wood with three wlekots in hand. The game was continued, and after Clarke had bowled Midwood, Podmore was responsible for the last two wickets, a brilliant running catch by Voi toy being loudly applauded, the innings closing for 121.

Of our junior terms, S. lamas' victory over Rich- mond's at Wilderspool stands out prominent, due in great part to the Ellison' excellent howling. 531128 neat batting was also shewn by Patrick, Ellison, and Scott. Miller's score ot thirteen was the best of the losing team.

The Sankey wire men tried conclusions with Runcorn, to the defeat of the latter on their own pitch. In Run- corn's Score of 28, Bean's batting, for 12 was very good. Evan's 18, and Woodcock's 9 were the beg contribu- tions to the winning team. Simpson's bowling was chiefly respondible for the comparatively low score of Runcorn.

Runcorn suffered a reverse in the viiit o° their 2nd team to Padgate.although C. Burrows bowled so well for them. taking 6 wickets for 17 runs. Walker made a good stand for the local team. His 20 runs was a very considerable proportion of the total score of 36.

The match between the first teatns of the Cheihire Lines Engmaers and Hough Green on the ground of the latter, ended in a win for the Engineers by 13 runs. Duckwortles score of 20 was very creditab'e. For Hough Green, Walker male 18 runs,t he next best being Dr. Mercer's 7 (not out). When we consider but 8 wickets went down for the total score, there it not much be- tween these teams.
\ CYCLING.

On Saturday last the Warrington Cycling Club's fix- ture was an inter-club run with the Manchester wheelers but owing to the destination not being fixed till Friday, the members decided to run to Marbury Hall. The turn- out numbered over 30, and a most enjoyable afternoon was spent. The run with the " Wheelers" will take place later in the season the place selected being Daven- ham.

A gentleman, evidently a military man from his ap- pearance, staying the night at one of our local hotels, told the writer he found cycling an admirable substitute for hunting. He had ridden down from Scotland, via. the Lake District, in easy stages of about forty miles a day,and was passing through Warrington towards Sur. rey. He would probably be about 50 years of age, ap- peared quite six feet in Welt, well buil:, and was in splendid condition. I venture to think few young man would undertake such a lonely journey from choice. He had ridden from Scotland before, but by a different route to Surrey.

Nothing tends to spoil the easy running of a cycle sooner than a loose bracket bearing ; the axle rocks,and the rocking motion is conveyed to the sprocket wheel, with the result that the chain is never in line, causing extra friction. Thera is also &considerable vibration on the pedals ;in fact, toe discomfort is so great that a rider changing from a properly-adjusted machine to one with a loose bracket cannot help noticing the difference. These bearings have a natural tendency to wear at the points, where the greatest pressdre comes on the pedals, and if the bracket is allowed to run loose for any length of time, the bearings are apt to become oval, and cannot , then be properly anjusted ; this should convince you of ' the necessity of keeping this particular bearing quite firm. To adjust the beacket ,which, I presume, is of tho barrel variety, hosen the bolt which goes through the split lug or is screwed inGo a slight projction on the opposite side to the chain, then insert a peg-hole wrench lin the two small holes and screw up the cup until the bearing is firm, after which the bolt which holds the cup in place must be firmly screwed up. Should the cup de- I cline to turn with the persuasive aid of the peg-hole wrench, it may he necessary to get a small punch, and placing it on the edge of one of the holes tap it with a I hammer until the bearing moves. At the Crystal Palace track on Monday, J. Platt Bette (Catford C.C.) in an attack on the mile record of lnaln. 35 2-5 secs.(flying start) succeeded in beating the quarter 1 of a mile record of 23 1-saec.(by J. W. Stocks) by 1-ssec. Betts' time being 23see. On a second attempt Betts tied the flying quarter, gnd succeeded in beating the half , naile by 2-53e5., the three quarter by 4-ssec., and the Imile by 2.53ec. Platt Betts's time were :—Quarter mile 23sec.; halt mile. 483 54ec.; threequarters, lmin. 103. ssec.; and mile, lmin. 35sees., as against J. W. Stock's record of lrnin.3s 2.saec.Betts also beat Lornbart's kilo- metre record of 58 4.53ec. by 1-slec., Betts's time being 58 3-siec. Mr. G. Pembroke Coleman,N.C.U.. timed.

GOLDEN Ptranniat.—Take a quarter of a pound each of marmalade,suet, bread ciumbri,and sugar. Put all the ingredients into a basin (having chopped the suet finely) stir well together,and moisten with two eggs well beaten and mixed with two tablespoonfuls of milk. It should be boiled for two hours, in a greased mould, tied down with a floured cloth, " MADGE."
